**Cochabamba** ([Aymara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_language "Aymara language"): _Quchapampa Jach'a Suyu_, [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Departamento de Cochabamba_ pronounced[[kotʃaˈβamba]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/9/95/ES-pe_-_Cochabamba.ogg/ES-pe_-_Cochabamba.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ES-pe_-_Cochabamba.ogg "File:ES-pe - Cochabamba.ogg"), [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_language "Quechua language"): _Quchapampa Suyu_), from Quechua _qucha_ or _qhucha_, meaning "lake", _pampa_ meaning "plain",[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-3) is one of the nine departments of Bolivia. It is known to be the [breadbasket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breadbasket "Breadbasket") of the country because of its variety of agricultural products from its geographical position. It has an area of 55,631 km 2. Its population in the 2024 census was 2,005,373. Its capital is the city of [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba "Cochabamba"), known as the "City of Eternal Spring" and "The Garden City" because of its spring-like temperatures all year.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Cochabamba valley has been inhabited for over a thousand years due to its fertile productive soils and climate. Archaeological evidence suggests that the initial valley inhabitants were of various ethnic indigenous groups. [Tiwanaku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiwanaku "Tiwanaku"), Tupuraya, Mojocoya, Omereque and [Inca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca "Inca") inhabited the valley at various times before the Spanish arrived.

The first Spanish inhabitant of the Valley was Garci Ruiz de Orellana in 1542. He purchased the majority of the land from local tribal chiefs Achata and Consavana through a title registered in 1552 at the Imperial City of Potosí. The price paid was 130 pesos. His residence, known as the House of Mayorazgo, still stands in the Cala Cala neighbourhood of the city.

The city, called Villa de Oropesa was founded on 2 August 1571 by order of Viceroy Francisco de Toledo, Count of Oropesa. It was to be an agricultural production centre to provide food for the mining towns of the relatively nearby Altiplano region, particularly the city of Potosí which became one of the largest and richest cities in the world during the 17th century– funding the vast wealth that ultimately made Spain a world power at the time. With the silver mining industry in Potosi at its height, Cochabamba thrived during its first centuries of existence. The city entered a period of decline during the 18th century as mining began to wane.

In 1786, King Charles III of Spain renamed the city to the 'loyal and valiant' Villa of Cochabamba. This was done to commend the city's pivotal role in suppressing the indigenous rebellions of 1781 in Oruro by sending armed forces to Oruro to quell the uprisings. Since the late 19th century it has again been generally successful as an agricultural centre for Bolivia.

The 1793 census shows that the city had a population of 22,305 persons. There were 12,980 mestizos, 6,368 Spaniards, 1,182 indigenous natives, 1,600 mulattos and 175 African slaves.

In 2000, Cochabamba was wracked by large-scale protests over the privatisation of the city's water supply, known as the [Water War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Water_War "Cochabamba Water War").

In January 2007 city dwellers clashed with mostly rural protestors, leaving four dead and over 130 injured. The democratically elected Prefect of Cochabamba, Manfred Reyes Villa, a former military aide to the Luis García Meza dictatorship of the 1980s, had allied himself with the leaders of Bolivia's eastern departments in a dispute with President Evo Morales over regional autonomy and other political issues. The protestors blockaded the highways, bridges, and main roads, having days earlier set fire to the departmental seat of government, trying to force the resignation of Reyes Villa. Citizens attacked the protestors, breaking the blockade and routing them, while the police did little to stop the violence. Further attempts by the protestors to reinstate the blockade and threaten the government were unsuccessful, but the underlying tensions have not been resolved.

In July 2007, a monument erected by veterans of January's protest movement in honour of those killed and injured by government supporters was destroyed in the middle of the night, reigniting racial conflicts in the city.

In August 2008, a nationwide referendum was held, and while President Evo Morales had 67% support in Bolivia, the Prefect of Cochabamba, Manfred Reyes Villa, was not confirmed by the voters of the department.

In 2018 Cochabamba hosted the 2018 South American Games ODESUR.

Around 74% of Cochabambinos identify as indigenous, while most of the remaining population is mestizo.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-4)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geography")]

Cochabamba Department is bordered by [Chuquisaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department "Chuquisaca Department") and [Potosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi_Department "Potosi Department") Departments to the south, [Oruro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oruro_Department "Oruro Department") and [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz_Department,_Bolivia "La Paz Department, Bolivia") Departments to the west, [Beni Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department "Beni Department") to the north, and [Santa Cruz Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia) "Santa Cruz Department (Bolivia)") to the east. The borders are formed mainly by rivers, like **Ichilo** to the east, **Rio Grande** to the south and **Cotacajes** to the west.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-5)

[![Image 9: Map of Cochabamba showing tree-cover loss years, with forest remaining since 2000 in green and loss years shaded yellow through purple.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Cochabamba%2C_2001-2024.png/330px-Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Cochabamba%2C_2001-2024.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Cochabamba,_2001-2024.png)

Tree-cover loss year in Cochabamba, 2001-2024, from the [Global Forest Change dataset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Forest_Change_dataset "Global Forest Change dataset").

Geographically and climatically, Cochabamba is one of Bolivia's most diverse regions, with a similar orography and diversity to [La Paz department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz_Department_(Bolivia) "La Paz Department (Bolivia)"). Cochabamba is made up of a variety of regions. The northern portions of the department, known as the Chapare, is a region of moist [Southwestern Amazonian moist forests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwestern_Amazonian_moist_forests "Southwestern Amazonian moist forests") with high levels of precipitation between 2,000mm and 7,000mm a year. This region is marked by steep hills and mountains at the edge of the Central Andes descending into the flat floodplains of the Llanos de Moxos to the north of Cochabamba. Further east of this region is a transition zone between the Tropical Wet-and-Dry forests of Santa Cruz and the Chapare, where Monsoonal climates predominate with an average annual precipitation between 1,800mm and 3,000mm.

South of the Tropical lowlands of Cochabamba lies a thin band of montane cloud forests that run slightly southeast from north to south in Cochabamba. This region features an unusual [subtropical highland climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical_highland_climate "Subtropical highland climate") and [Oceanic climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_climate "Oceanic climate"), with precipitation year-round, with some drying periods. Precipitation in this region ranges between 1,000mm and 2,500mm.

The center of the department is marked by the temperate xeric valleys of Cochabamba (known as Kanata), Alto Cochabamba, and Capinota. These valley areas are marked by dry montane forests, and semi-arid orographies. Temperate climates year-round feature considerable diurnal temperature variation due to the high altitude. A majority of the department's population lives in this area, where major cities are located like [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba "Cochabamba"), [Cliza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cliza_(town) "Cliza (town)"), [Punata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punata "Punata"), [Sacaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacaba "Sacaba"), [Quillacollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quillacollo "Quillacollo"), [Arani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arani,_Bolivia "Arani, Bolivia"), [Santivańez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiva%C5%84ez?action=edit&redlink=1 "Santivańez (page does not exist)"), [Capinota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capinota "Capinota"), [Irpa Irpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irpa_Irpa "Irpa Irpa"), among others.

Surrounding the smaller valleys of the department's center from the west to the east, is a region of Andean highlands, featuring a [subtropical highland climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical_highland_climate "Subtropical highland climate"), with annual precipitation averaging between 400mm and 1,400mm. This region of rocky valleys and moderately sized mountains features mosaics of high altitude forests and agricultural heartland. This region features dramatic and diverse geographies, with a considerable historical and archaeological importance.

To the southeast of the highlands of Cochabamba, are semi-arid valleys and mountains terminating at the banks of the Wapaymayu or Río Grande. This area, famous for its cultural history, is marked by dry valleys and mountains, with agricultural lands bordering rivers throughout the region. Precipitation in this region is generally sparse, oscillating between 300mm and 600mm per year, bordering on a [Desert climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desert_climate "Desert climate")

To the extreme southwest, is a small tract of Puna which features a cold [Tundra climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tundra_climate "Tundra climate"), with unusual subpolar oceanic characteristics. Precipitation in this area ranges between 300mm and 650mm per year.

## Government

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Government")]

### Executive offices

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Executive offices")]

Since May 2010, the chief executive officer of Bolivia departments has been the governor; before then, the officer was called the prefect, and until 2006, the prefect was appointed by the [president of Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Bolivia "President of Bolivia"). The current governor, Humberto Sánchez of the [Movement for Socialism– Political Instrument for the Sovereignty of the Peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_for_Socialism_%E2%80%93_Political_Instrument_for_the_Sovereignty_of_the_Peoples "Movement for Socialism – Political Instrument for the Sovereignty of the Peoples") (MAS–IPSP) was elected on 7 March 2021 and took office on 4 May.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-6)

The MAS–IPSP has been the dominant political party in the department since the 2008 recall referendum.

### Legislative Assembly

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Legislative Assembly")]

Under the [2009 Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_Constitution_of_2009 "Bolivian Constitution of 2009"), Bolivian departments have an elected legislature, the Departmental Legislative Assembly. The Cochabamba Assembly has 34 members including two indigenous representatives. The [first elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_regional_election,_2010#Chuquisaca "Bolivian regional election, 2010") were held 4 April 2010 and the current composition was determined at the [regional election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Bolivian_regional_elections "2021 Bolivian regional elections") on 7 March 2021.

The current executive committee, elected on 3 May 2022, consists of Elena Aine Espinoza as president, Francisco Otalora Ticona as first vice-president, Pedro Andrés Badran Leon as second vice-president and Julieta Veizaga Guevara as first secretary.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-9)

### Regions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Regions")]

The municipalities in Cochabamba Department can also be grouped informally into large regions.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-13) Provinces are not subsumed under regions, which have rather different borders. The five regions are:

*   Región Andina (lit.'Andean Region' or 'Region of the Andes'): the [cordilleras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera "Cordillera") in the west, part of the [Altiplano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altiplano "Altiplano").
*   Cono Sur (lit.'Southern Cone'), a cone-shaped (vaguely triangular) corner in the southeast.
*   [Región Metropolitana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanata_Metropolitan_Area "Kanata Metropolitan Area"): the department's most populous region, centered around the capital city, [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba "Cochabamba")
*   Trópico (el Trópico de Cochabamba): the department's largest region, including [Chimoré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimor%C3%A9,_Cochabamba "Chimoré, Cochabamba"), [Colomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colomi "Colomi"), [Entre Rios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entre_Rios,_Cochabamba "Entre Rios, Cochabamba"), [Puerto Villarroel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Villarroel "Puerto Villarroel"), [Shinahota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinahota "Shinahota"), [Villa Tunari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villa_Tunari "Villa Tunari"), and part of the _[llanos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llanos "Llanos") tropicales_
*   Valles (lit.'Valleys'): south of Metropolitana.

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Economy")]

The Cochabamba economy is based mainly in services, but recently it is experiencing some diversification in manufacturing, agriculture and tourism. The geographic location of Cochabamba makes it the main routes of transport joining the two main cities, the host government La Paz and the industrial hub Santa Cruz. Therefore, many cervices i.e. transport, banking, telecommunication, gastronomy, are economically important in the corridor La Paz – Santa Cruz. Extraction of oil was very important for the economy in the past; especially in Chapare where the wells are located. By 2013 many of the exploited wells were showing signs of depletion. Thus, investment is needed to find new productive wells. Once called “the basket grain of Bolivia” today Cochabamba produces just a portion of the agriculture output of the country. Overpopulation in the productive valleys and “minifundio” doomed the once competitive production. Nevertheless, Cochabamba is still important in poultry, dairy, tropical fruits, potatoes, among others. Recently, Cochabamba experiences some improvement in manufacturing and industry. The cement mill of COBOCE located in Capinota almost triples the production tapering the strong demand. The roads to the industrial park and other facilities of the park were improved making it more competitive for the local and new industries. Also, it is worth to mention the almost 1b USD government investment in the petro chemistry (urea plant) located in Bulo Bulo.

**Cochabamba** ([Aymara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_language "Aymara language"): _Quchapampa Jach'a Suyu_, [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Departamento de Cochabamba_ pronounced[[kotʃaˈβamba]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/9/95/ES-pe_-_Cochabamba.ogg/ES-pe_-_Cochabamba.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ES-pe_-_Cochabamba.ogg "File:ES-pe - Cochabamba.ogg"), [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_language "Quechua language"): _Quchapampa Suyu_), from Quechua _qucha_ or _qhucha_, meaning "lake", _pampa_ meaning "plain",[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-3) is one of the nine departments of Bolivia. It is known to be the [breadbasket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breadbasket "Breadbasket") of the country because of its variety of agricultural products from its geographical position. It has an area of 55,631 km 2. Its population in the 2024 census was 2,005,373. Its capital is the city of [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba "Cochabamba"), known as the "City of Eternal Spring" and "The Garden City" because of its spring-like temperatures all year.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Cochabamba valley has been inhabited for over a thousand years due to its fertile productive soils and climate. Archaeological evidence suggests that the initial valley inhabitants were of various ethnic indigenous groups. [Tiwanaku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiwanaku "Tiwanaku"), Tupuraya, Mojocoya, Omereque and [Inca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca "Inca") inhabited the valley at various times before the Spanish arrived.

The first Spanish inhabitant of the Valley was Garci Ruiz de Orellana in 1542. He purchased the majority of the land from local tribal chiefs Achata and Consavana through a title registered in 1552 at the Imperial City of Potosí. The price paid was 130 pesos. His residence, known as the House of Mayorazgo, still stands in the Cala Cala neighbourhood of the city.

The city, called Villa de Oropesa was founded on 2 August 1571 by order of Viceroy Francisco de Toledo, Count of Oropesa. It was to be an agricultural production centre to provide food for the mining towns of the relatively nearby Altiplano region, particularly the city of Potosí which became one of the largest and richest cities in the world during the 17th century– funding the vast wealth that ultimately made Spain a world power at the time. With the silver mining industry in Potosi at its height, Cochabamba thrived during its first centuries of existence. The city entered a period of decline during the 18th century as mining began to wane.

In 1786, King Charles III of Spain renamed the city to the 'loyal and valiant' Villa of Cochabamba. This was done to commend the city's pivotal role in suppressing the indigenous rebellions of 1781 in Oruro by sending armed forces to Oruro to quell the uprisings. Since the late 19th century it has again been generally successful as an agricultural centre for Bolivia.

The 1793 census shows that the city had a population of 22,305 persons. There were 12,980 mestizos, 6,368 Spaniards, 1,182 indigenous natives, 1,600 mulattos and 175 African slaves.

In 2000, Cochabamba was wracked by large-scale protests over the privatisation of the city's water supply, known as the [Water War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Water_War "Cochabamba Water War").

In January 2007 city dwellers clashed with mostly rural protestors, leaving four dead and over 130 injured. The democratically elected Prefect of Cochabamba, Manfred Reyes Villa, a former military aide to the Luis García Meza dictatorship of the 1980s, had allied himself with the leaders of Bolivia's eastern departments in a dispute with President Evo Morales over regional autonomy and other political issues. The protestors blockaded the highways, bridges, and main roads, having days earlier set fire to the departmental seat of government, trying to force the resignation of Reyes Villa. Citizens attacked the protestors, breaking the blockade and routing them, while the police did little to stop the violence. Further attempts by the protestors to reinstate the blockade and threaten the government were unsuccessful, but the underlying tensions have not been resolved.

In July 2007, a monument erected by veterans of January's protest movement in honour of those killed and injured by government supporters was destroyed in the middle of the night, reigniting racial conflicts in the city.

In August 2008, a nationwide referendum was held, and while President Evo Morales had 67% support in Bolivia, the Prefect of Cochabamba, Manfred Reyes Villa, was not confirmed by the voters of the department.

In 2018 Cochabamba hosted the 2018 South American Games ODESUR.

Around 74% of Cochabambinos identify as indigenous, while most of the remaining population is mestizo.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-4)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geography")]

Cochabamba Department is bordered by [Chuquisaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department "Chuquisaca Department") and [Potosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi_Department "Potosi Department") Departments to the south, [Oruro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oruro_Department "Oruro Department") and [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz_Department,_Bolivia "La Paz Department, Bolivia") Departments to the west, [Beni Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department "Beni Department") to the north, and [Santa Cruz Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia) "Santa Cruz Department (Bolivia)") to the east. The borders are formed mainly by rivers, like **Ichilo** to the east, **Rio Grande** to the south and **Cotacajes** to the west.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-5)

[![Image 9: Map of Cochabamba showing tree-cover loss years, with forest remaining since 2000 in green and loss years shaded yellow through purple.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Cochabamba%2C_2001-2024.png/330px-Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Cochabamba%2C_2001-2024.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Cochabamba,_2001-2024.png)

Tree-cover loss year in Cochabamba, 2001-2024, from the [Global Forest Change dataset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Forest_Change_dataset "Global Forest Change dataset").

Geographically and climatically, Cochabamba is one of Bolivia's most diverse regions, with a similar orography and diversity to [La Paz department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz_Department_(Bolivia) "La Paz Department (Bolivia)"). Cochabamba is made up of a variety of regions. The northern portions of the department, known as the Chapare, is a region of moist [Southwestern Amazonian moist forests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwestern_Amazonian_moist_forests "Southwestern Amazonian moist forests") with high levels of precipitation between 2,000mm and 7,000mm a year. This region is marked by steep hills and mountains at the edge of the Central Andes descending into the flat floodplains of the Llanos de Moxos to the north of Cochabamba. Further east of this region is a transition zone between the Tropical Wet-and-Dry forests of Santa Cruz and the Chapare, where Monsoonal climates predominate with an average annual precipitation between 1,800mm and 3,000mm.

South of the Tropical lowlands of Cochabamba lies a thin band of montane cloud forests that run slightly southeast from north to south in Cochabamba. This region features an unusual [subtropical highland climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical_highland_climate "Subtropical highland climate") and [Oceanic climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_climate "Oceanic climate"), with precipitation year-round, with some drying periods. Precipitation in this region ranges between 1,000mm and 2,500mm.

The center of the department is marked by the temperate xeric valleys of Cochabamba (known as Kanata), Alto Cochabamba, and Capinota. These valley areas are marked by dry montane forests, and semi-arid orographies. Temperate climates year-round feature considerable diurnal temperature variation due to the high altitude. A majority of the department's population lives in this area, where major cities are located like [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba "Cochabamba"), [Cliza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cliza_(town) "Cliza (town)"), [Punata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punata "Punata"), [Sacaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacaba "Sacaba"), [Quillacollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quillacollo "Quillacollo"), [Arani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arani,_Bolivia "Arani, Bolivia"), [Santivańez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiva%C5%84ez?action=edit&redlink=1 "Santivańez (page does not exist)"), [Capinota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capinota "Capinota"), [Irpa Irpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irpa_Irpa "Irpa Irpa"), among others.

Surrounding the smaller valleys of the department's center from the west to the east, is a region of Andean highlands, featuring a [subtropical highland climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical_highland_climate "Subtropical highland climate"), with annual precipitation averaging between 400mm and 1,400mm. This region of rocky valleys and moderately sized mountains features mosaics of high altitude forests and agricultural heartland. This region features dramatic and diverse geographies, with a considerable historical and archaeological importance.

To the southeast of the highlands of Cochabamba, are semi-arid valleys and mountains terminating at the banks of the Wapaymayu or Río Grande. This area, famous for its cultural history, is marked by dry valleys and mountains, with agricultural lands bordering rivers throughout the region. Precipitation in this region is generally sparse, oscillating between 300mm and 600mm per year, bordering on a [Desert climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desert_climate "Desert climate")

To the extreme southwest, is a small tract of Puna which features a cold [Tundra climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tundra_climate "Tundra climate"), with unusual subpolar oceanic characteristics. Precipitation in this area ranges between 300mm and 650mm per year.

### Legislative Assembly

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Legislative Assembly")]

Under the [2009 Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_Constitution_of_2009 "Bolivian Constitution of 2009"), Bolivian departments have an elected legislature, the Departmental Legislative Assembly. The Cochabamba Assembly has 34 members including two indigenous representatives. The [first elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_regional_election,_2010#Chuquisaca "Bolivian regional election, 2010") were held 4 April 2010 and the current composition was determined at the [regional election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Bolivian_regional_elections "2021 Bolivian regional elections") on 7 March 2021.

The current executive committee, elected on 3 May 2022, consists of Elena Aine Espinoza as president, Francisco Otalora Ticona as first vice-president, Pedro Andrés Badran Leon as second vice-president and Julieta Veizaga Guevara as first secretary.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-9)

### Regions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Regions")]

The municipalities in Cochabamba Department can also be grouped informally into large regions.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department#cite_note-13) Provinces are not subsumed under regions, which have rather different borders. The five regions are:

*   Región Andina (lit.'Andean Region' or 'Region of the Andes'): the [cordilleras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera "Cordillera") in the west, part of the [Altiplano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altiplano "Altiplano").
*   Cono Sur (lit.'Southern Cone'), a cone-shaped (vaguely triangular) corner in the southeast.
*   [Región Metropolitana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanata_Metropolitan_Area "Kanata Metropolitan Area"): the department's most populous region, centered around the capital city, [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba "Cochabamba")
*   Trópico (el Trópico de Cochabamba): the department's largest region, including [Chimoré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimor%C3%A9,_Cochabamba "Chimoré, Cochabamba"), [Colomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colomi "Colomi"), [Entre Rios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entre_Rios,_Cochabamba "Entre Rios, Cochabamba"), [Puerto Villarroel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Villarroel "Puerto Villarroel"), [Shinahota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinahota "Shinahota"), [Villa Tunari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villa_Tunari "Villa Tunari"), and part of the _[llanos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llanos "Llanos") tropicales_
*   Valles (lit.'Valleys'): south of Metropolitana.

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba_Department&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Economy")]

The Cochabamba economy is based mainly in services, but recently it is experiencing some diversification in manufacturing, agriculture and tourism. The geographic location of Cochabamba makes it the main routes of transport joining the two main cities, the host government La Paz and the industrial hub Santa Cruz. Therefore, many cervices i.e. transport, banking, telecommunication, gastronomy, are economically important in the corridor La Paz – Santa Cruz. Extraction of oil was very important for the economy in the past; especially in Chapare where the wells are located. By 2013 many of the exploited wells were showing signs of depletion. Thus, investment is needed to find new productive wells. Once called “the basket grain of Bolivia” today Cochabamba produces just a portion of the agriculture output of the country. Overpopulation in the productive valleys and “minifundio” doomed the once competitive production. Nevertheless, Cochabamba is still important in poultry, dairy, tropical fruits, potatoes, among others. Recently, Cochabamba experiences some improvement in manufacturing and industry. The cement mill of COBOCE located in Capinota almost triples the production tapering the strong demand. The roads to the industrial park and other facilities of the park were improved making it more competitive for the local and new industries. Also, it is worth to mention the almost 1b USD government investment in the petro chemistry (urea plant) located in Bulo Bulo.

**Santa Cruz** (Spanish pronunciation:[[ˌsanta ˈkɾus]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")) is the largest of the nine constituent departments of [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"), occupying about one-third (33.74%) of the country's territory. With an area of 370,621 km 2 (143,098 sq mi), it is slightly smaller than [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") or the [US](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") state of [Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montana "Montana"). It is located in the eastern part of the country, sharing borders in the north and east with [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil") and with [Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguay "Paraguay") in the south.

In the 2024 census, it had an estimated population of 3.1 million, making it the most populated department. Its capital city is [Santa Cruz de la Sierra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra "Santa Cruz de la Sierra"). The department is one of the wealthiest departments in Bolivia, with huge [reserves of natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas_in_Bolivia "Natural gas in Bolivia"). Besides, it has experienced the highest increase of economic growth during the last 50 years in Bolivia and South America.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Government and administration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Government and administration")]

See also: [List of senators of Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_senators_of_Santa_Cruz "List of senators of Santa Cruz")

According to the current [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Bolivia "Constitution of Bolivia"), the highest authority in the department lies with the [governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor "Governor"). The former figure of prefect was appointed by the [President of the Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Bolivia "President of Bolivia") till 2005, when the prefect for the first time was elected by popular vote to serve for a five-year term. In 2010 the first governor was elected according to the implementation of autonomy after a struggle for almost a decade by the people of Santa Cruz.

Santa Cruz also has a Departmental Assembly _(Asamblea Departamental),_ which derives but differs from the previous Departmental Council _(Consejo Departamental)._ It is a state legislature with limited legislation powers, being able to make laws in certain subjects in exclusivity and in some others in concurrence with the state legislative branch.

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Economy")]

Satellite images of western [Chiquitos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiquitos_Province "Chiquitos Province") and southern [Ñuflo de Chávez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%91uflo_de_Ch%C3%A1vez_Province "Ñuflo de Chávez Province") provinces illustrate deforestation from agrarian expansion.

The department covers a vast expanse of territory in eastern Bolivia, much of it [rainforests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainforest "Rainforest"), extending from the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") to the border with [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"). The department's economy depends largely on [agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture "Agriculture"), with [sugar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar "Sugar"), [cotton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotton "Cotton"), [soybeans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soybean "Soybean") and [rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice "Rice") being grown. The amount of land cultivated by modern farming techniques is increasing rapidly in the Santa Cruz area, where weather allows for two crops a year.

In recent years,[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] the [discovery of natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas_in_Bolivia "Natural gas in Bolivia") in the department has led to plans for the development of a regional natural gas industry that is likely to boost the local economy. Bolivia's energy minister said two proposed [liquefied petroleum gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquefied_petroleum_gas "Liquefied petroleum gas") plants may allow the country to boost supplies to Brazil and Argentina by 2010, easing a shortage of the fuel after a lack of investment reduced output. The processing plants would be built in Santa Cruz and each would produce about 200 tons of liquefied petroleum gas a day. The plants would help turn a deficit of gas into a “surplus”.

In July 2004, the people voted in a nationwide [referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referendum "Referendum") to allow for regulated exportation of the gas.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-3)

The department also hosts [El Mutún](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Mut%C3%BAn "El Mutún"), the world's second largest iron ore reserve (after Carajás in Brazil) and largest [magnesium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesium "Magnesium") deposits are also located there. Located in the Germán Busch Province in the Santa Cruz Department of Bolivia, near Puerto Suárez, El Mutún extends across the border into Brazil, where it is called the Serrania de Jacadigo. Also known as the "Serrania Mutún", it has an area of about 75 square kilometers. Its estimated reserves are about 40.205 billion tons of iron ore of 50% iron, mainly in hematite and magnetite form, and in lesser quantities in siderite and manganese minerals. This can be compared with an estimate of the total world reserves of iron ore: 800 billion tons of crude ore containing more than 230 billion tons of iron.

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Geography")]

Santa Cruz Department is the largest of the Bolivian departments and covers a wide and diverse area. In the west lies a series of temperate Sub-Andean ranges and valleys while to the north and south lies two different lowlands areas; the Beni and [Chaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran_Chaco "Gran Chaco") lowlands respectively. To the northeast lies the flat [Llanos Chiquitanos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llanos_Chiquitanos?action=edit&redlink=1 "Llanos Chiquitanos (page does not exist)") areas and beyond these the [Serranías Chiquitanas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serran%C3%ADas_Chiquitanas "Serranías Chiquitanas") ranges. In the far east the departments have small parts of the huge [Pantanal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantanal "Pantanal") wetland.

The rivers of Santa Cruz are part of any of two basins: the [Amazon Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Basin "Amazon Basin") (north) and the [Plate Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_Basin?action=edit&redlink=1 "Plate Basin (page does not exist)") (south).

The main rivers in the northern basin are [river Iténez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_It%C3%A9nez "River Iténez"), making the border with Brazil, [Río Grande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%ADo_Grande_(Bolivia) "Río Grande (Bolivia)"), [river Piraí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pira%C3%AD_River_(Bolivia) "Piraí River (Bolivia)") and [river Itonomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Itonomas "River Itonomas"). In the southern basin, the main rivers are [river Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Paraguay "River Paraguay") and its tributaries, including [river Negro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Negro_(Boivia-Paraguay)?action=edit&redlink=1 "River Negro (Boivia-Paraguay) (page does not exist)").

The main lakes are [lake Mandioré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Mandior%C3%A9 "Lake Mandioré"), Uberaba, [lake La Gaiba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_La_Gaiba "Lake La Gaiba"), [Laguna de Marfil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_de_Marfil "Laguna de Marfil"), Concepción and [lake San Jorge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_San_Jorge "Lake San Jorge").

## Demographics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Demographics")]

The first settlers of Santa Cruz were mainly [Spaniards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaniards "Spaniards") that accompanied Ñuflo de Chávez, as well as [Guarani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guarani_people "Guarani people"), and some [Flemings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flemish_people "Flemish people"), [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_people "Portuguese people"), [Germans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_people "German people") and [Italians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_people "Italian people") working for the Spanish crown.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-4) Among the first settlers there were also [Sephardic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sephardic "Sephardic")[Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-5) recently converted to [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") who were persecuted by the [Inquisition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inquisition "Inquisition") in Spain. Santa Cruz has a multicultural population: 57% are [Mestizos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo") with both Indigenous Amazonian and European ascendants, 30% are Natives ([Chiquitano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiquitano_people "Chiquitano people"), [Chane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chane_people "Chane people"), [Ayoreo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayoreo_people "Ayoreo people"), as well as Quechua and Aymara internal migrants from other departments) and 13% are [Whites of European descent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Bolivians "White Bolivians"), of whom about a third are the so-called ["Russian" Mennonites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Mennonite "Russian Mennonite") (see [Mennonites in Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mennonites_in_Bolivia "Mennonites in Bolivia")) of [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germans "Germans") tradition, language and descent.

## Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Climate")]

At 416 meters above sea level, it is warm and tropical most of the year. Winters are short and last only 2–3 months but can get very cold very suddenly. "Surazos" (southerly winds that blow in from Argentina) can drop the temperature by as much as 30 degrees overnight. This extreme cold lasts only a few days at a time and the beautiful, sub-tropical Santa Cruz is pleasant throughout most of the year. Here the climate varies by geographical zone: temperate to cold in the western sierras and warm to hot and humid as one descends into the extensive plains.

The department of Santa Cruz regularly experiences devastating forest fires, often started by landowners who want to burn forests to create new agricultural land. This practice puts a great strain on the rich biodiversity of the country.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-7)

## Calls for autonomy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Calls for autonomy")]

During the later stages of the [Chaco war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaco_war "Chaco war") between Paraguay and Bolivia, as the Paraguayan army approached Santa Cruz department, local nationalists backed by a Paraguay-based independence movement sought to create a separate independent state in Santa Cruz department.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-9)

[A referendum on autonomy was held in Santa Cruz department in 2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_autonomy_referendum,_2008 "Santa Cruz autonomy referendum, 2008"). Eastern departments in Bolivia, including Santa Cruz, have majority of the natural gas reserves. Bolivian president Evo Morales was planning to introduce legislation to tackle the poverty in the country using tax revenues from richer departments like Santa Cruz. Additionally, Morales's attempts to change the constitution were opposed by the opposition governors who run five of Bolivia's nine regions.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-10) 85.6 percent voted in favour of autonomy. The Bolivian government considered the referendum illegal.

**Santa Cruz** (Spanish pronunciation:[[ˌsanta ˈkɾus]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")) is the largest of the nine constituent departments of [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"), occupying about one-third (33.74%) of the country's territory. With an area of 370,621 km 2 (143,098 sq mi), it is slightly smaller than [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") or the [US](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") state of [Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montana "Montana"). It is located in the eastern part of the country, sharing borders in the north and east with [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil") and with [Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguay "Paraguay") in the south.

In the 2024 census, it had an estimated population of 3.1 million, making it the most populated department. Its capital city is [Santa Cruz de la Sierra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra "Santa Cruz de la Sierra"). The department is one of the wealthiest departments in Bolivia, with huge [reserves of natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas_in_Bolivia "Natural gas in Bolivia"). Besides, it has experienced the highest increase of economic growth during the last 50 years in Bolivia and South America.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Government and administration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Government and administration")]

See also: [List of senators of Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_senators_of_Santa_Cruz "List of senators of Santa Cruz")

According to the current [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Bolivia "Constitution of Bolivia"), the highest authority in the department lies with the [governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor "Governor"). The former figure of prefect was appointed by the [President of the Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Bolivia "President of Bolivia") till 2005, when the prefect for the first time was elected by popular vote to serve for a five-year term. In 2010 the first governor was elected according to the implementation of autonomy after a struggle for almost a decade by the people of Santa Cruz.

Santa Cruz also has a Departmental Assembly _(Asamblea Departamental),_ which derives but differs from the previous Departmental Council _(Consejo Departamental)._ It is a state legislature with limited legislation powers, being able to make laws in certain subjects in exclusivity and in some others in concurrence with the state legislative branch.

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Economy")]

[![Image 12: Satellite image 1984](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/LandSat-Chiquitos%2C_Santa_Cruz%2C_Bolivia_1984.jpg/250px-LandSat-Chiquitos%2C_Santa_Cruz%2C_Bolivia_1984.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LandSat-Chiquitos,_Santa_Cruz,_Bolivia_1984.jpg)

1984

[![Image 13: Satellite image 1984](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/LandSat-Chiquitos%2C_Santa_Cruz%2C_Bolivia_2000.jpg/250px-LandSat-Chiquitos%2C_Santa_Cruz%2C_Bolivia_2000.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LandSat-Chiquitos,_Santa_Cruz,_Bolivia_2000.jpg)

2000

Satellite images of western [Chiquitos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiquitos_Province "Chiquitos Province") and southern [Ñuflo de Chávez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%91uflo_de_Ch%C3%A1vez_Province "Ñuflo de Chávez Province") provinces illustrate deforestation from agrarian expansion.

The department covers a vast expanse of territory in eastern Bolivia, much of it [rainforests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainforest "Rainforest"), extending from the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") to the border with [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"). The department's economy depends largely on [agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture "Agriculture"), with [sugar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar "Sugar"), [cotton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotton "Cotton"), [soybeans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soybean "Soybean") and [rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice "Rice") being grown. The amount of land cultivated by modern farming techniques is increasing rapidly in the Santa Cruz area, where weather allows for two crops a year.

In recent years,[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] the [discovery of natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas_in_Bolivia "Natural gas in Bolivia") in the department has led to plans for the development of a regional natural gas industry that is likely to boost the local economy. Bolivia's energy minister said two proposed [liquefied petroleum gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquefied_petroleum_gas "Liquefied petroleum gas") plants may allow the country to boost supplies to Brazil and Argentina by 2010, easing a shortage of the fuel after a lack of investment reduced output. The processing plants would be built in Santa Cruz and each would produce about 200 tons of liquefied petroleum gas a day. The plants would help turn a deficit of gas into a “surplus”.

In July 2004, the people voted in a nationwide [referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referendum "Referendum") to allow for regulated exportation of the gas.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-3)

The department also hosts [El Mutún](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Mut%C3%BAn "El Mutún"), the world's second largest iron ore reserve (after Carajás in Brazil) and largest [magnesium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesium "Magnesium") deposits are also located there. Located in the Germán Busch Province in the Santa Cruz Department of Bolivia, near Puerto Suárez, El Mutún extends across the border into Brazil, where it is called the Serrania de Jacadigo. Also known as the "Serrania Mutún", it has an area of about 75 square kilometers. Its estimated reserves are about 40.205 billion tons of iron ore of 50% iron, mainly in hematite and magnetite form, and in lesser quantities in siderite and manganese minerals. This can be compared with an estimate of the total world reserves of iron ore: 800 billion tons of crude ore containing more than 230 billion tons of iron.

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 14: Map of Santa Cruz showing tree-cover loss years, with forest remaining since 2000 in green and loss years shaded yellow through purple.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Santa_Cruz%2C_2001-2024.png/330px-Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Santa_Cruz%2C_2001-2024.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Santa_Cruz,_2001-2024.png)

Tree-cover loss year in Santa Cruz, 2001-2024, from the [Global Forest Change dataset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Forest_Change_dataset "Global Forest Change dataset").

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Forest%2C_Santa_Criz_Dept%2C_Bolivia.jpg/250px-Forest%2C_Santa_Criz_Dept%2C_Bolivia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Forest,_Santa_Criz_Dept,_Bolivia.jpg)

Aerial photo of forest, Santa Cruz Department, 2009.

Santa Cruz Department is the largest of the Bolivian departments and covers a wide and diverse area. In the west lies a series of temperate Sub-Andean ranges and valleys while to the north and south lies two different lowlands areas; the Beni and [Chaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran_Chaco "Gran Chaco") lowlands respectively. To the northeast lies the flat [Llanos Chiquitanos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llanos_Chiquitanos?action=edit&redlink=1 "Llanos Chiquitanos (page does not exist)") areas and beyond these the [Serranías Chiquitanas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serran%C3%ADas_Chiquitanas "Serranías Chiquitanas") ranges. In the far east the departments have small parts of the huge [Pantanal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantanal "Pantanal") wetland.

The rivers of Santa Cruz are part of any of two basins: the [Amazon Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Basin "Amazon Basin") (north) and the [Plate Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_Basin?action=edit&redlink=1 "Plate Basin (page does not exist)") (south).

The main rivers in the northern basin are [river Iténez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_It%C3%A9nez "River Iténez"), making the border with Brazil, [Río Grande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%ADo_Grande_(Bolivia) "Río Grande (Bolivia)"), [river Piraí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pira%C3%AD_River_(Bolivia) "Piraí River (Bolivia)") and [river Itonomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Itonomas "River Itonomas"). In the southern basin, the main rivers are [river Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Paraguay "River Paraguay") and its tributaries, including [river Negro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Negro_(Boivia-Paraguay)?action=edit&redlink=1 "River Negro (Boivia-Paraguay) (page does not exist)").

The main lakes are [lake Mandioré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Mandior%C3%A9 "Lake Mandioré"), Uberaba, [lake La Gaiba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_La_Gaiba "Lake La Gaiba"), [Laguna de Marfil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_de_Marfil "Laguna de Marfil"), Concepción and [lake San Jorge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_San_Jorge "Lake San Jorge").

## Demographics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Demographics")]

The first settlers of Santa Cruz were mainly [Spaniards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaniards "Spaniards") that accompanied Ñuflo de Chávez, as well as [Guarani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guarani_people "Guarani people"), and some [Flemings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flemish_people "Flemish people"), [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_people "Portuguese people"), [Germans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_people "German people") and [Italians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_people "Italian people") working for the Spanish crown.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-4) Among the first settlers there were also [Sephardic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sephardic "Sephardic")[Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-5) recently converted to [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") who were persecuted by the [Inquisition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inquisition "Inquisition") in Spain. Santa Cruz has a multicultural population: 57% are [Mestizos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo") with both Indigenous Amazonian and European ascendants, 30% are Natives ([Chiquitano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiquitano_people "Chiquitano people"), [Chane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chane_people "Chane people"), [Ayoreo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayoreo_people "Ayoreo people"), as well as Quechua and Aymara internal migrants from other departments) and 13% are [Whites of European descent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Bolivians "White Bolivians"), of whom about a third are the so-called ["Russian" Mennonites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Mennonite "Russian Mennonite") (see [Mennonites in Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mennonites_in_Bolivia "Mennonites in Bolivia")) of [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germans "Germans") tradition, language and descent.

## Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Climate")]

At 416 meters above sea level, it is warm and tropical most of the year. Winters are short and last only 2–3 months but can get very cold very suddenly. "Surazos" (southerly winds that blow in from Argentina) can drop the temperature by as much as 30 degrees overnight. This extreme cold lasts only a few days at a time and the beautiful, sub-tropical Santa Cruz is pleasant throughout most of the year. Here the climate varies by geographical zone: temperate to cold in the western sierras and warm to hot and humid as one descends into the extensive plains.

The department of Santa Cruz regularly experiences devastating forest fires, often started by landowners who want to burn forests to create new agricultural land. This practice puts a great strain on the rich biodiversity of the country.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-7)

## Calls for autonomy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_Department&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Calls for autonomy")]

During the later stages of the [Chaco war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaco_war "Chaco war") between Paraguay and Bolivia, as the Paraguayan army approached Santa Cruz department, local nationalists backed by a Paraguay-based independence movement sought to create a separate independent state in Santa Cruz department.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-9)

[A referendum on autonomy was held in Santa Cruz department in 2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_autonomy_referendum,_2008 "Santa Cruz autonomy referendum, 2008"). Eastern departments in Bolivia, including Santa Cruz, have majority of the natural gas reserves. Bolivian president Evo Morales was planning to introduce legislation to tackle the poverty in the country using tax revenues from richer departments like Santa Cruz. Additionally, Morales's attempts to change the constitution were opposed by the opposition governors who run five of Bolivia's nine regions.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia)#cite_note-10) 85.6 percent voted in favour of autonomy. The Bolivian government considered the referendum illegal.

**Arani** is a [province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_Bolivia "Provinces of Bolivia") in Cochabamba Department, [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"). Its capital is [Arani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arani_(Bolivia) "Arani (Bolivia)"), situated about 53 km from [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba "Cochabamba"). Arani is known for its bread and its artisan wickerwork.

Arani Municipality consists of three cantons, Arani, Pocoata and Collpaciaco. Vacas Municipality is not further subdivided, so Vacas Canton and Vacas Municipality are identical.

## Tourism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Arani_Province&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Tourism")]

Festivals and Fairs:

*   August 14–15: [Saint Isidore the Laborer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isidore_the_Laborer "Isidore the Laborer") in Qullpayaku, 2 days
*   August 24–25: _Virgen la Bella_ in Arani, 2 days
*   September 20: Farmers' fair in [Tacopaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacopaya "Tacopaya"), 1 day
*   3rd week in November: Bread fair in Arani, 1 day
*   December 4: [Saint Barbara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Barbara "Saint Barbara") in [Vacas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacas_(Cochabamba) "Vacas (Cochabamba)")

Other tourist attractions include the church of [Saint Bartholomew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartholomew_the_Apostle "Bartholomew the Apostle") (_San Bartolomé_) in Arani, built in 1610, which is dedicated to the _Virgen la Bella_, and the lakes in Vacas Municipality: [Parqu Qucha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parqu_Qucha_(Bolivia) "Parqu Qucha (Bolivia)"), [Asiru Qucha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asiru_Qucha_(Bolivia) "Asiru Qucha (Bolivia)"), Junt'utuyu, [Pilawit'u](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilawit'u "Pilawit'u"), [Qullpa Qucha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qullpa_Qucha "Qullpa Qucha") and Yanatama.

**Arani** is a [province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_Bolivia "Provinces of Bolivia") in Cochabamba Department, [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"). Its capital is [Arani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arani_(Bolivia) "Arani (Bolivia)"), situated about 53 km from [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba "Cochabamba"). Arani is known for its bread and its artisan wickerwork.

## Subdivision

The province is divided into two [municipalities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipalities_of_Bolivia "Municipalities of Bolivia") which are further subdivided into four [cantons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantons_of_Bolivia "Cantons of Bolivia").

Arani Municipality consists of three cantons, Arani, Pocoata and Collpaciaco. Vacas Municipality is not further subdivided, so Vacas Canton and Vacas Municipality are identical.

## Tourism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Arani_Province&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Tourism")]

Festivals and Fairs:

*   August 14–15: [Saint Isidore the Laborer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isidore_the_Laborer "Isidore the Laborer") in Qullpayaku, 2 days
*   August 24–25: _Virgen la Bella_ in Arani, 2 days
*   September 20: Farmers' fair in [Tacopaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacopaya "Tacopaya"), 1 day
*   3rd week in November: Bread fair in Arani, 1 day
*   December 4: [Saint Barbara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Barbara "Saint Barbara") in [Vacas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacas_(Cochabamba) "Vacas (Cochabamba)")

Other tourist attractions include the church of [Saint Bartholomew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartholomew_the_Apostle "Bartholomew the Apostle") (_San Bartolomé_) in Arani, built in 1610, which is dedicated to the _Virgen la Bella_, and the lakes in Vacas Municipality: [Parqu Qucha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parqu_Qucha_(Bolivia) "Parqu Qucha (Bolivia)"), [Asiru Qucha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asiru_Qucha_(Bolivia) "Asiru Qucha (Bolivia)"), Junt'utuyu, [Pilawit'u](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilawit'u "Pilawit'u"), [Qullpa Qucha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qullpa_Qucha "Qullpa Qucha") and Yanatama.

**Cochabamba** ([Aymara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_language "Aymara language") and [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_language "Quechua language"): _Quchapampa_) is a city and municipality in central [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia") in a valley in the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") mountain range. It is the capital of the Cochabamba Department and the [fourth largest city in Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_and_largest_towns_in_Bolivia "List of cities and largest towns in Bolivia"), with a population of 661,484 according to the [2024 Bolivian census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Bolivian_census "2024 Bolivian census").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-4) Its name is from a compound of the [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_languages "Quechua languages") words _qucha_ "lake" and _[pampa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pampa "Pampa")_, "open plain."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-5) Residents of the city and the surrounding areas are commonly referred to as _cochalas_ or, more formally, _cochabambinos_.

It is known as the "City of Eternal Spring" or "The Garden City" because of its spring-like temperatures all year round.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-6) It is also known as "La Llajta," which means "town" in Quechua. It is the largest urban center between the higher capital of [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz "La Paz") and [Santa Cruz de la Sierra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra "Santa Cruz de la Sierra") in the tropical plains of the east. It sits south-west of the Tunari mountains, and north of the foothills of the Valle Alto. In antiquity, the area featured numerous lakes, which gave the city its name. Many of these lakes have since disappeared to urban development, but Coña Coña and Alalay lakes are extant examples. It has been a populated settlement since the Pre-Inca period, and is today an important cultural, educational, political, and commercial centre.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Pre-Inca and Inca

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Pre-Inca and Inca")]

The valley of Cochabamba has been inhabited for thousands of years due to its fertile productive [soils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil "Soil") and mild [climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate "Climate"). [Archaeological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archeology "Archeology") evidence suggests that the initial inhabitants were of indigenous ethnic groups: [Tiwanaku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiwanaku "Tiwanaku"), Tupuraya, Mojocoya, [Omereque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omereque "Omereque"), and [Inca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca "Inca") inhabited the valley at times before the Spanish arrived.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The name Cochabamba is a Spanish spelling of the [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_languages "Quechua languages") compound noun qucha pampa (literally 'lake plain', [phonemically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoneme "Phoneme") /qutʃa pampa/, [phonetically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonetics "Phonetics") [ˈqɔtʃa ˈpampa]). Under the [Inca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca "Inca") Empire, the area was conquered by [Topa Inca Yupanqui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topa_Inca_Yupanqui "Topa Inca Yupanqui") (ruled 1471–1493). His son [Huayna Capac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huayna_Capac "Huayna Capac") turned Cochabamba into a large production enclave or state farm to serve the Incas. The local population was possibly depleted during the Inca conquest and Huayna Capac imported 14,000 people, called [mitimas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitima "Mitima"), to work the land. The principal crop was maize which could not be grown in much of the high and cold heartland of the Inca Empire. The maize was stored in 2,400 storehouses ([qollqas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qollqa "Qollqa")) in the hills overlooking the valley or transported by [llama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llama "Llama") caravan to storage sites in [Paria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paria,_Bolivia "Paria, Bolivia"), [Cusco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cusco "Cusco"), of other Inca administrative centres. Most of the maize was probably used to sustain the Inca army during its campaigns.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-8)

### Spanish and Bolivian

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Spanish and Bolivian")]

The first Spanish inhabitant of the valley was Garci Ruiz de Orellana in 1542. He purchased the majority of the land from local tribal chiefs Achata and Consavana through a title registered in 1552 at the Imperial City of [Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD "Potosí"). The price paid was 130 pesos. His residence, known as the House of Mayorazgo, still stands in the Cala Cala neighbourhood.

The city, called Villa de Oropesa, was founded in January 1571 by order of [Viceroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceroy "Viceroy")[Francisco de Toledo, Count of Oropesa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_de_Toledo,_Count_of_Oropesa "Francisco de Toledo, Count of Oropesa").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-9) It was to be an agricultural production centre to provide food and wood for the mining towns of the relatively nearby [Altiplano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altiplano "Altiplano") region, particularly [Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD "Potosí") which became one of the largest and richest cities in the world during the 16th and 17th centuries — funding the vast wealth that ultimately made Spain a world power. In fact, anthropologist Jack Weatherford and others have cited the city of Potosí as the birth of capitalism because of the money and materialism it provided Spain.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-10) Thus, with the [silver mining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_mining "Silver mining") industry in Potosí at its height, Cochabamba thrived during its first centuries. However, the city entered a period of decline during the 18th century as mining began to wane.

In 1786 King [Charles III of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_III_of_Spain "Charles III of Spain") renamed the city the 'loyal and valiant' Villa of Cochabamba. This was done to commend the city's pivotal role in suppressing the indigenous rebellions of 1781 in [Oruro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oruro,_Bolivia "Oruro, Bolivia") by sending armed forces to Oruro to quell the uprisings. Since the late 19th century it has again been generally successful as an agricultural centre for Bolivia.

The 1793 census shows that the city had a population of 22,305 persons. There were 12,980 [mestizos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizos "Mestizos"), 6,368 Spaniards, 1,182 indigenous natives, 1,600 [mulattos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mulattos "Mulattos") and 175 African slaves.

In 1812 Cochabamba was the site of a riot against the Spanish Army. On May 27, thousands of women took up arms against the Spanish. According to historian Nathaniel Aguirre: "From Cochabamba, many men have fled. Not one woman. On the hillside, a great clamour. Cochabamba's plebeian women, at bay, fight from the centre of a circle of fire. Surrounded by five thousand Spaniards, they resist with battered tin guns and a few arquebuses; and they fight to the last yell, whose echoes will resound throughout the long war for independence. Whenever his army weakens, General Manuel Belgrano will shout those words which never fail to restore courage and spark anger. The general will ask his vacillating soldiers: '_Are the women of Cochabamba present?_"[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-11)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_]

To celebrate their bravery, Bolivia now marks May 27 as Mother's Day.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-12)

In 1900 the population was 21,886.

Besides a number of schools and charitable institutions, the Catholic diocese has 55 parishes, 80 churches and chapels, and 160 priests.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1998 the International Monetary Fund agreed to give Bolivia a loan of $138 million to control inflation and promote economic growth. But it only agreed to do so on the condition that Bolivia sell "all remaining public enterprises," including its national oil refineries and the local water company, SEMAPA.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-:0-13) In 1999, a group of private investors, specifically the Bechtel Corporation with headquarters in San Francisco, California, United States of America, came together under the name of Aguas del Tunari and bought the rights for the privatization of the city's water.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-14) In that same year, the World Bank (WB) refused to subsidize the water to help lower the cost for the people. Then in 2000, the people of Cochabamba began to protest as water priced hiked to a 50% increase that the majority could not afford.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-:1-15)

The Coalition for the Defense of Water and Life, and its leader Oscar Olivera, started a demonstration in _La Plaza 14 de Septiembre_ also known as _La Plaza Principal._ The march was meant to be peaceful, but after two days the police used tear gas against the protestors and injured about 175 people and killed 1 and blinded two. Soon after, news reports were made about the protests and the violence.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-:0-13) The Defense of Water and Life held an unofficial referendum and 96% of 50,000 people wanted Aguas del Tunari's contract to terminate, but the government refused. The protests only grew and the entire world began to watch forcing Bechtel to leave its contract and return SEMAPA to the public. Bechtel as well tried to sue the Bolivian government for $50 million but it withdrew its claim shortly after.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-:1-15) This event was soon labelled as the Water Wars and became a driving force for anti-globalization projects such as the UN's decision to make water sanitation a human right and the privatisation of water as unethical in 2010. Additionally, the Water Wars would help spark the next revolt against the privatisation of natural gases from 2003 to 2005 which would lead to the removal of two presidents, Gonzalo Sánchez de Lozada and Carlos Mesa, and the rise of President Evo Morales in 2006.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-16)

In January 2007 city dwellers clashed with mostly rural protestors, leaving four dead and over 130 injured.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The first democratically elected Prefect of Cochabamba, [Manfred Reyes Villa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Reyes_Villa "Manfred Reyes Villa"), had allied himself with the leaders of Bolivia's Eastern Departments in a dispute with President [Evo Morales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evo_Morales "Evo Morales") over regional autonomy and other political issues. The protestors blockaded the highways, bridges, and main roads, having days earlier set fire to the departmental seat of government, trying to force the resignation of Reyes Villa. Citizens attacked the protestors, breaking the blockade and routing them, while the police did little to stop the violence. Further attempts by the protestors to reinstate the blockade and threaten the government were unsuccessful, but the underlying tensions had not been resolved.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In July 2007 a monument erected by veterans of January's protest movement in honour of those killed and injured by government supporters was destroyed in the middle of the night, reigniting racial conflicts in the city.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In August 2008 a nationwide referendum was held. The prefect of Cochabamba, Manfred Reyes Villa, was not confirmed by the voters, and he was removed from the position.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Climate and geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Climate and geography")]

Cochabamba is known for its "Eternal Spring". Neither experiencing the humid heat of [Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra "Santa Cruz de la Sierra") nor the frigid winds of [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz "La Paz"), Cochabamba experiences a [semi-arid climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_semi-arid_climate "Cold semi-arid climate") ([Köppen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen-Geiger_climate_classification_system "Köppen-Geiger climate classification system"): _BSk_), bordering on a [subtropical highland climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical_highland_climate "Subtropical highland climate") ([Köppen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen-Geiger_climate_classification_system "Köppen-Geiger climate classification system"): _Cwb_). The characteristic of the climate is an extended dry season that runs from May until October with a wet season that generally begins in November with the principal rains ending in March.

The valley of Cochabamba has been classified as a [mesothermal valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesothermal_valley "Mesothermal valley").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-geohi-17) The basin floor has an average elevation of 2600 m but at its lowest point in the east it runs at 2480 m.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-geohi-17) Surrounding mountains vary in height with the highest elevation in vicinity of valley being [Tunari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunari_(Bolivia) "Tunari (Bolivia)") with 5,023 m a.s.l.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-geohi-17) The city is primarily built on the [Cenozoic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenozoic "Cenozoic") and more specifically, [Quaternary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternary "Quaternary")[sedimentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sediment "Sediment") fill of the basin-valley.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-geohi-17) Mountains and hills are composed of old rocks dating to the [Paleozoic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleozoic "Paleozoic") and, in some parts, to the [Cretaceous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretaceous "Cretaceous").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-geohi-17)

According to the 2024 Bolivian census, the population of the municipality of Cochabamba is 665,505 inhabitants.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-27) This makes it the fourth most populous municipality in the country, behind [Santa Cruz de la Sierra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra "Santa Cruz de la Sierra"), [El Alto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Alto "El Alto"), and [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz "La Paz").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-28)

The population of the municipality increased by more than half between 1992 and 2024:
