At the beginning of the republican era, Cochabamba ranked as the second most populated city in Bolivia according to the 1846 census, with a total of 30,396 inhabitants, behind La Paz, which had more than 60,000 inhabitants at that time.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-29)

The city extends beyond the political-administrative boundaries of the municipality of Cochabamba, forming a conurbation with the municipalities of [Colcapirhua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colcapirhua_Municipality "Colcapirhua Municipality"), [Quillacollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quillacollo_Municipality "Quillacollo Municipality"), [Sacaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacaba "Sacaba"), [Sipe Sipe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sipe_Sipe_Municipality "Sipe Sipe Municipality"), [Tiquipaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiquipaya_Municipality "Tiquipaya Municipality"), and [Vinto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinto_Municipality "Vinto Municipality"). Together they make up the Kanata Metropolitan Region, which is the third-largest metropolitan area in Bolivia and an important tourist, economic, industrial, and population center.

Like other Bolivian urban centers, Cochabamba is no exception to the national trend of urban growth at the expense of the rural population. This process of accelerated urbanization is not due exclusively to industrialization, but also to complex political and social factors such as poverty, the decline of the agricultural sector, and the availability of job opportunities in cities.

## Culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Culture")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Cultura_Cochabambina.jpg/250px-Cultura_Cochabambina.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cultura_Cochabambina.jpg)

Traditional clothing of Cochabamba

In Cochabamba, one of the most important religious festivities in Bolivia is held: that of the Virgin of Urkupiña, also known as the Patroness of National Integration. This celebration brings together Catholics from all over the country as well as foreign pilgrims, who participate either as spectators or as dancers in the folkloric procession of the same name, immersing themselves in the dual nature of a religious and traditional celebration. Another important festivity is the Alasitas Fair and the Corso de Corsos.

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Silpancho_cochalo.jpg/250px-Silpancho_cochalo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Silpancho_cochalo.jpg)

_[Sillp’ancho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silpancho "Silpancho") cochabambino_

The cuisine of Cochabamba is characterized by its great variety of culinary dishes. Since 2017, Cochabamba has been part of UNESCO's Creative Cities Network in the category of gastronomy.

*   **Chicharrón**: a dish made with pork cooked for approximately 5 to 6 hours, served with cooked corn hominy (_mote_) and potatoes.
*   **P’ampaku**: a dish prepared with chicken, pork, duck, potato, sweet potato, and plantain. All these ingredients are placed in a hermetically sealed container and buried in a pit, which is covered with stones and bricks previously heated by a wood or charcoal fire until the stones crack. It is covered with fresh grass or banana leaves and then completely sealed with mud. The food is considered cooked when the pit cracks and smoke rises from the burned fresh grass. It is served with a fresh vegetable salad.
*   **Pichón de Cliza**: a dish made with pigeon meat (squab), boiled and then grilled. It is served with rice and boiled potatoes.
*   **[Sillp’ancho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silpancho "Silpancho")**: a dry dish with breaded beef, pan-fried, accompanied by a fried egg and a raw salad of onion, carrot, tomato, and _locoto_. It is served with rice and boiled potatoes, which are later sliced and fried.
*   **Lapping**: a dish with fried marinaded flank steak.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-30)
*   **Jak’a Lawa**: a dish made from ground _choclo_ (fresh corn on the cob), accompanied by pieces of meat and pork rind. It is served in a deep plate.
*   **Ch’aqchu**: a dish made with _chuño_, meat boiled in water with potatoes and fava beans, hard-boiled eggs, fresh cheese sliced into rounds, and a salad of tomato and raw onion, all topped with a spicy red chili sauce.
*   **Jawas Piqtu**: a dish made with fava beans mixed with egg and tomato. It is served with potatoes.
*   **Pique Macho**: originally a dish made of beef loin fried in its own juices, with French fries, and a salad of tomato, onion, _locoto_, and sliced hard-boiled egg. The French fries are placed on the plate first, then the meat and chorizo are mixed and placed on top, and finally the salad and egg. A typical accompaniment is a mixture of oil, vinegar, salt, _llajua_, and finally beer, all mixed in a glass and then poured over the dish.
*   **Chank’a de conejo**: rabbit meat cut into pieces and boiled together with a white soup containing green onion (scallion), white potato, vegetables, and seasoned with traditional _llajwa_.
*   **Uchuku Aiquileño**: a dish consisting of red chili pepper, potatoes, rice, _chuño_, and meats (beef tongue, duck, and chicken). It is served with a chicken soup with chili (thickened with trimmings or ground bread), accompanied by rice cake, _ch’uñu phuti_, potato cake, fried ceibo flowers (_chilliqchi_), white potatoes, chicken meat, beef tongue, and golden-browned duck.
*   **[Llajua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llajua "Llajua")**: a spicy sauce made from _locoto_, tomato, and _quilquiña_ (an aromatic herb). The vast majority of traditional Bolivian dishes are accompanied by this sauce.

The international street art festival known as the BAU (Bienal de Arte Urbano) has been hosted in Cochabamba every two years since 2011. The festival is organized by proyecto mARTadero, a local cultural centre. In 2011, 2013, 2015, and 2017 the painting was done in the Villa Coronilla, and Geronimo de Osorio neighbourhoods. In 2019 the festival focused on the neighbourhood Esperanza, on the edge of the [Alalay Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alalay_Lake "Alalay Lake"). The festival has featured internationally renowned artists such as [Blu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blu_(artist) "Blu (artist)") (Italy) and Inti (Chile).[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-31)

Commensurate with other large cities in the Andean highlands of South America, Cochabamba is a city of contrasts. Its central commercial districts, Zona Norte, is bounded by Plaza Colón and Plaza 14 de Septiembre, are generally equipped with modern urban amenities and are where the majority of the city's formal business and commercial industries are based. La Cancha, the largest open-air market in South America, is also an active place where locals can buy a range of items.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-32) An active nightlife is centered around Calle España and along the broad, tree-lined boulevard, El Prado. In contrast, the Zona Sur, a remote area adjacent to the Wilstermann International Airport is visibly impoverished, with adobe homes and unpaved roads, which is often the first impression visitors acquire while commuting into the city.

In 2009, the government under President Evo Morales created a new constitution that declared Spanish and 36 other indigenous languages as the official languages of the country.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-:2-33) However, the most widely spoken languages in Cochabamba are Spanish and Quechua. Although the Spanish that is spoken in the Cochabamba region is generally regarded as rather conservative in its phonetics and vocabulary, the use of Quechua terminology (_wawa_ [child] and _wistupiku_ [mouth or twist lips][[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-34)) has been widely incorporated into its standardized form.

About four-fifths of the population of Bolivia identifies as Catholic.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-:2-33)

Like other cities that share the same ethnic group quadrants like [Salta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salta "Salta") or [Cuenca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuenca,_Ecuador "Cuenca, Ecuador"), Cochabamba's demographics consist of the following visible groups in order of prevalence: Indigenous (mostly of [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_people "Quechua people") and [Aymara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_people "Aymara people") ethnicity) people, [Mestizo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo"), or mixed Indigenous and Spanish European, and people of Spanish ([Criollos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criollo_(people) "Criollo (people)")) and other European descent. As well as a fairly significant population of [Afro-Bolivians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Bolivians "Afro-Bolivians").

By 2013, the human development index of the Metropolitan region of Cochabamba was 0.801 as a result of a 35% growth in the last 20 years.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-undp-3)

### Capital status

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Capital status")]

Cochabamba is the capital of the department of Cochabamba and the seat of the Autonomous Departmental Government of Cochabamba, the political and administrative authority of the department. Following the enactment of the Popular Participation Law No. 1551 in 1994, together with the Administrative Decentralization Law No. 1654, a process of reconfiguration between the State and civil society was initiated, transferring powers and resources to subnational levels, such as municipal governments. As a result, Bolivia's departments enjoy autonomy statutes that define their internal structure. At the parliamentary level, the executive branch is headed by a governor, while the legislative branch is exercised by a [departmental legislative assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Bolivia "Politics of Bolivia"). In addition to the governor's office and several directorates, the Autonomous Departmental Government of Cochabamba is made up of eight departmental secretariats.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-35) The status of being the capital constitutes a distinguishing factor in relation to the other cities of the department, due to the higher concentration of public officials and a larger floating population that comes to Cochabamba to carry out procedures with the different secretariats and directorates.

Cochabamba is also the capital of the [Cercado Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cercado_Province_(Cochabamba) "Cercado Province (Cochabamba)"), located in the center of the department, since its founding on August 15, 1571 by the Spanish captain Gerónimo de Osorio under the original name Villa Real de Oropesa.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-37) This means that the various provincial delegations of the departments of the Autonomous Departmental Government and institutions of the Government of Bolivia are located in the city.

### Municipal government

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Municipal government")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Alcald%C3%ADa_Municipal_de_Cbba.jpg/250px-Alcald%C3%ADa_Municipal_de_Cbba.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alcald%C3%ADa_Municipal_de_Cbba.jpg)

Cochabamba City Hall

The administration of the city is carried out through democratic governance, whose authorities are elected every four years by universal suffrage. The electoral roll is made up of all registered residents of Cochabamba who are over 18 years of age and Bolivian nationals. The Mayor of Cochabamba is the head of government and of the municipal administration, legally representing the municipality in judicial and extrajudicial matters. The mayor also presides over the executive branch of the city.

According to Article 283 of the Political Constitution of the State and Law No. 482 on Autonomous Municipal Governments, municipal government consists of the Municipal Council, which exercises legislative, deliberative, and oversight powers, in cooperation with the executive branch.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-38) The Cochabamba Municipal Council is composed of eleven councilors elected by direct vote in municipal elections and represents the highest legislative authority of the municipal government. Decisions and resolutions are adopted by a majority vote or by a two-thirds majority, depending on the general regulations.

Since May 3, 2021, the Mayor of Cochabamba has been former presidential candidate and businessman [Manfred Reyes Villa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Reyes_Villa "Manfred Reyes Villa") ([APB Súmate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/APB_S%C3%BAmate "APB Súmate")).[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-39)

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Economy")]

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Muyurina%2C_Cochabamba.jpg/250px-Muyurina%2C_Cochabamba.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Muyurina,_Cochabamba.jpg)

Muyurina Skyline 

Cochabamba ranks third in economic importance nationwide. Historically, Cochabamba's economy was supported by agriculture. Currently, it has diversified and relies more on oil production and manufacturing. The municipality's economy is primarily centered on the [tertiary sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Services_sector "Services sector"), with activities such as commerce, transportation, storage, and other services, followed by the manufacturing industry. In 2021, the municipal Gross Domestic Product (GDP) was estimated to reach approximately 17,535 million [bolivianos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boliviano_(currency)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Boliviano (currency) (page does not exist)") (equivalent to US$6,710 million in [purchasing power parity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purchasing_power_parity "Purchasing power parity") terms), with a [GDP per capita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GDP_per_capita "GDP per capita") of 20,844 bolivianos (US$7,977 PPP).[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-:2-33) According to these figures, the municipality's economy contributes 43.6% of the department's value added and 6% of the national economy. During the heyday of the mining industry in [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"), Cochabamba enjoyed sustained development, only to enter a period of decline during the 18th century, as the silver mining industry began to decline. However, during the second half of the 19th century it was established as an agricultural center in the country.

The city's central area is where most of its businesses and commercial activity is concentrated. A large amount of formal and informal commerce is present on the streets of Cochabamba, encompassing the popular commercial area known as [La Cancha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Cancha "La Cancha"), made up of several private and public markets. However, its growth has begun to displace the commercial center to the northwest of the city, traditionally considered a residential area. It has a vibrant cosmopolitan nightlife, especially around Calle España and along the boulevard or avenue El Prado.

The city is home to many of the country's largest and most important companies, such as Boliviana de Aviación, ELFEC, Comteco, MotorParts, IC Norte, and large establishments such as Hipermaxi, Paseo Aranjuez, Hupermall, Supermall, and Mall Brisas del Sur, among others.

Cochabamba is the third-largest economy in Bolivia and is the most stable due to the dynamism of its market and domestic consumption, as well as its excellent transportation system, which allows it to transport goods to all of the department's provinces.

At the end of April and beginning of May of each year, the [Alalay Fairgrounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alalay_Fairgrounds?action=edit&redlink=1 "Alalay Fairgrounds (page does not exist)") opens its doors for eleven days exclusively to hold trade fair events of all kinds, with FEICOBOL (Cochabamba International Fair) being one of the largest commercial events in [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia") and its activities brought together companies worldwide, which helped the economy of the department and the growth of tourism. It was currently replaced by the Cochabamba International Exhibition Fair or FEXCO in an agreement between the [Autonomous Municipal Government of Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_Municipal_Government_of_Cochabamba?action=edit&redlink=1 "Autonomous Municipal Government of Cochabamba (page does not exist)") and the Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Services of Cochabamba (ICAM), which began its activities with its first version, held in 2023.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-40)

### Agriculture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Agriculture")]

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Cochabamba_1988.jpg/250px-Cochabamba_1988.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cochabamba_1988.jpg)

The Cochabamba Valley around 1987

Agriculture in the city of Cochabamba was very important, but it has declined due to the expansion of the urban area, which has reduced the arable land south of the city, to the Maica and Tamborada areas. However, in the city's markets, you can buy products that vary depending on the area from which they are brought, from regions with a distant climate and geography:

*   **The Tropics**: in this area, the crops of [banana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musa_%C3%97_paradisiaca "Musa × paradisiaca"), orange, [mandarin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandarin_orange "Mandarin orange"), palm heart, papaya, pineapple, cocoa, etc. are mainly found.
*   **The valleys**, this is the main agricultural area, in this area there are crops of [broad bean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicia_faba "Vicia faba"), [pea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pisum_sativum "Pisum sativum"), onion, corn, tomato, [locoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locoto "Locoto"), [parsley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsley "Parsley"), lettuce, [turnip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turnip "Turnip"), carrot, [custard apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Custard_apple "Custard apple"), [strawberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fragaria "Fragaria"), [peach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prunus_persica "Prunus persica"), etc.

*   **Subyungas**, in this area there are mainly crops of [broad bean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicia_faba "Vicia faba"), peas, custard apple and potato.

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Transport")]

The metropolitan area of Cochabamba (Vinto, Tiquipaya, Quillacollo, Colcapirhua, Cochabamba and Sacaba) has an extensive transportation system, which cover all the districts.

There are almost 70 bus and minibus lines, from A to Z, and dozens of minibuses and fixed-route trufis (T.RU.FI, or "taxi con ruta fija") taxi lines. Most lines have [GPS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPS "GPS") system for monitoring and regulation of hour (line 1, line 16, line L, Line 3V, line 20, line 30, etc.). The T.RU.FI service has at least 60 lines; they are identified by signs on the roof of the vehicle showing the route from the initial stop until the final stop, which is also indicated by the line number to which it belongs.

## Municipal waste

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Municipal waste")]

EMSA, the municipal sanitation company, is responsible for the pickup, transportation, storage and removed from urban waste produced. EMSA covers 88% of the city and collects 400 tonnes of waste produced per day.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-Botaderos18Apr-42) Through the municipal government of Cochabamba, special containers made available throughout the city for the storage of solid waste common. The municipality's sole disposal facility, the K'ara K'ara waste dump (Botadero K'ara K'ara), has been the centre of a long-running controversy over pollution of the air and groundwater; it is frequently blockaded by neighbouring residents demanding changes.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-Botaderos18Apr-42)

## Additional notes of interest

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Additional notes of interest")]

*   Cochabamba is also mentioned in the documentary _[The Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Corporation\_(2003\_film) "The Corporation (2003 film)")_, about their fight against the privatisation of water by a foreign-owned company, against which the people protested and won. The privatisation had gone to such an extent that even rainwater was not allowed to be collected. Read [Cochabamba protests of 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_protests_of_2000 "Cochabamba protests of 2000").
*   Cochabamba was featured as a location in the story in the 1983 film, _[Scarface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarface\_(1983\_film) "Scarface (1983 film)")_. Powerful drug lord [Alejandro Sosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alejandro_Sosa "Alejandro Sosa") resided there, governed large coca plantations and owned cocaine labs whereupon further refining, would be shipped to [Tony Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Montana "Tony Montana") in Florida.
*   Cochabamba is the setting of the 2010 movie _[También la Lluvia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tambi%C3%A9n\_la\_Lluvia "También la Lluvia")_ (_Even the rain_), which takes place during the water war of 2000. It depicts a crew making a movie about the colonization of Latin America when the protests against privatization erupt. The film stars Mexican actor [Gael García Bernal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gael_Garc%C3%ADa_Bernal "Gael García Bernal"), and received positive reviews.
*   Cochabamba is also the site of several major spammers, as confirmed by the watchdog group Spamhaus.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-43)

**Cochabamba** ([Aymara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_language "Aymara language") and [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_language "Quechua language"): _Quchapampa_) is a city and municipality in central [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia") in a valley in the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") mountain range. It is the capital of the Cochabamba Department and the [fourth largest city in Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_and_largest_towns_in_Bolivia "List of cities and largest towns in Bolivia"), with a population of 661,484 according to the [2024 Bolivian census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Bolivian_census "2024 Bolivian census").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-4) Its name is from a compound of the [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_languages "Quechua languages") words _qucha_ "lake" and _[pampa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pampa "Pampa")_, "open plain."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-5) Residents of the city and the surrounding areas are commonly referred to as _cochalas_ or, more formally, _cochabambinos_.

It is known as the "City of Eternal Spring" or "The Garden City" because of its spring-like temperatures all year round.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-6) It is also known as "La Llajta," which means "town" in Quechua. It is the largest urban center between the higher capital of [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz "La Paz") and [Santa Cruz de la Sierra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra "Santa Cruz de la Sierra") in the tropical plains of the east. It sits south-west of the Tunari mountains, and north of the foothills of the Valle Alto. In antiquity, the area featured numerous lakes, which gave the city its name. Many of these lakes have since disappeared to urban development, but Coña Coña and Alalay lakes are extant examples. It has been a populated settlement since the Pre-Inca period, and is today an important cultural, educational, political, and commercial centre.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Pre-Inca and Inca

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Pre-Inca and Inca")]

The valley of Cochabamba has been inhabited for thousands of years due to its fertile productive [soils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil "Soil") and mild [climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate "Climate"). [Archaeological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archeology "Archeology") evidence suggests that the initial inhabitants were of indigenous ethnic groups: [Tiwanaku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiwanaku "Tiwanaku"), Tupuraya, Mojocoya, [Omereque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omereque "Omereque"), and [Inca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca "Inca") inhabited the valley at times before the Spanish arrived.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The name Cochabamba is a Spanish spelling of the [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_languages "Quechua languages") compound noun qucha pampa (literally 'lake plain', [phonemically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoneme "Phoneme") /qutʃa pampa/, [phonetically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonetics "Phonetics") [ˈqɔtʃa ˈpampa]). Under the [Inca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca "Inca") Empire, the area was conquered by [Topa Inca Yupanqui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topa_Inca_Yupanqui "Topa Inca Yupanqui") (ruled 1471–1493). His son [Huayna Capac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huayna_Capac "Huayna Capac") turned Cochabamba into a large production enclave or state farm to serve the Incas. The local population was possibly depleted during the Inca conquest and Huayna Capac imported 14,000 people, called [mitimas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitima "Mitima"), to work the land. The principal crop was maize which could not be grown in much of the high and cold heartland of the Inca Empire. The maize was stored in 2,400 storehouses ([qollqas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qollqa "Qollqa")) in the hills overlooking the valley or transported by [llama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llama "Llama") caravan to storage sites in [Paria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paria,_Bolivia "Paria, Bolivia"), [Cusco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cusco "Cusco"), of other Inca administrative centres. Most of the maize was probably used to sustain the Inca army during its campaigns.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-8)

### Spanish and Bolivian

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Spanish and Bolivian")]

The first Spanish inhabitant of the valley was Garci Ruiz de Orellana in 1542. He purchased the majority of the land from local tribal chiefs Achata and Consavana through a title registered in 1552 at the Imperial City of [Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD "Potosí"). The price paid was 130 pesos. His residence, known as the House of Mayorazgo, still stands in the Cala Cala neighbourhood.

The city, called Villa de Oropesa, was founded in January 1571 by order of [Viceroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceroy "Viceroy")[Francisco de Toledo, Count of Oropesa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_de_Toledo,_Count_of_Oropesa "Francisco de Toledo, Count of Oropesa").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-9) It was to be an agricultural production centre to provide food and wood for the mining towns of the relatively nearby [Altiplano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altiplano "Altiplano") region, particularly [Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD "Potosí") which became one of the largest and richest cities in the world during the 16th and 17th centuries — funding the vast wealth that ultimately made Spain a world power. In fact, anthropologist Jack Weatherford and others have cited the city of Potosí as the birth of capitalism because of the money and materialism it provided Spain.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-10) Thus, with the [silver mining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_mining "Silver mining") industry in Potosí at its height, Cochabamba thrived during its first centuries. However, the city entered a period of decline during the 18th century as mining began to wane.

In 1786 King [Charles III of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_III_of_Spain "Charles III of Spain") renamed the city the 'loyal and valiant' Villa of Cochabamba. This was done to commend the city's pivotal role in suppressing the indigenous rebellions of 1781 in [Oruro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oruro,_Bolivia "Oruro, Bolivia") by sending armed forces to Oruro to quell the uprisings. Since the late 19th century it has again been generally successful as an agricultural centre for Bolivia.

The 1793 census shows that the city had a population of 22,305 persons. There were 12,980 [mestizos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizos "Mestizos"), 6,368 Spaniards, 1,182 indigenous natives, 1,600 [mulattos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mulattos "Mulattos") and 175 African slaves.

In 1812 Cochabamba was the site of a riot against the Spanish Army. On May 27, thousands of women took up arms against the Spanish. According to historian Nathaniel Aguirre: "From Cochabamba, many men have fled. Not one woman. On the hillside, a great clamour. Cochabamba's plebeian women, at bay, fight from the centre of a circle of fire. Surrounded by five thousand Spaniards, they resist with battered tin guns and a few arquebuses; and they fight to the last yell, whose echoes will resound throughout the long war for independence. Whenever his army weakens, General Manuel Belgrano will shout those words which never fail to restore courage and spark anger. The general will ask his vacillating soldiers: '_Are the women of Cochabamba present?_"[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-11)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_]

To celebrate their bravery, Bolivia now marks May 27 as Mother's Day.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-12)

In 1900 the population was 21,886.

Besides a number of schools and charitable institutions, the Catholic diocese has 55 parishes, 80 churches and chapels, and 160 priests.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1998 the International Monetary Fund agreed to give Bolivia a loan of $138 million to control inflation and promote economic growth. But it only agreed to do so on the condition that Bolivia sell "all remaining public enterprises," including its national oil refineries and the local water company, SEMAPA.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-:0-13) In 1999, a group of private investors, specifically the Bechtel Corporation with headquarters in San Francisco, California, United States of America, came together under the name of Aguas del Tunari and bought the rights for the privatization of the city's water.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-14) In that same year, the World Bank (WB) refused to subsidize the water to help lower the cost for the people. Then in 2000, the people of Cochabamba began to protest as water priced hiked to a 50% increase that the majority could not afford.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-:1-15)

The Coalition for the Defense of Water and Life, and its leader Oscar Olivera, started a demonstration in _La Plaza 14 de Septiembre_ also known as _La Plaza Principal._ The march was meant to be peaceful, but after two days the police used tear gas against the protestors and injured about 175 people and killed 1 and blinded two. Soon after, news reports were made about the protests and the violence.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-:0-13) The Defense of Water and Life held an unofficial referendum and 96% of 50,000 people wanted Aguas del Tunari's contract to terminate, but the government refused. The protests only grew and the entire world began to watch forcing Bechtel to leave its contract and return SEMAPA to the public. Bechtel as well tried to sue the Bolivian government for $50 million but it withdrew its claim shortly after.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-:1-15) This event was soon labelled as the Water Wars and became a driving force for anti-globalization projects such as the UN's decision to make water sanitation a human right and the privatisation of water as unethical in 2010. Additionally, the Water Wars would help spark the next revolt against the privatisation of natural gases from 2003 to 2005 which would lead to the removal of two presidents, Gonzalo Sánchez de Lozada and Carlos Mesa, and the rise of President Evo Morales in 2006.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-16)

In January 2007 city dwellers clashed with mostly rural protestors, leaving four dead and over 130 injured.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The first democratically elected Prefect of Cochabamba, [Manfred Reyes Villa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Reyes_Villa "Manfred Reyes Villa"), had allied himself with the leaders of Bolivia's Eastern Departments in a dispute with President [Evo Morales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evo_Morales "Evo Morales") over regional autonomy and other political issues. The protestors blockaded the highways, bridges, and main roads, having days earlier set fire to the departmental seat of government, trying to force the resignation of Reyes Villa. Citizens attacked the protestors, breaking the blockade and routing them, while the police did little to stop the violence. Further attempts by the protestors to reinstate the blockade and threaten the government were unsuccessful, but the underlying tensions had not been resolved.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In July 2007 a monument erected by veterans of January's protest movement in honour of those killed and injured by government supporters was destroyed in the middle of the night, reigniting racial conflicts in the city.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In August 2008 a nationwide referendum was held. The prefect of Cochabamba, Manfred Reyes Villa, was not confirmed by the voters, and he was removed from the position.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Climate and geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Climate and geography")]

Cochabamba is known for its "Eternal Spring". Neither experiencing the humid heat of [Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra "Santa Cruz de la Sierra") nor the frigid winds of [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz "La Paz"), Cochabamba experiences a [semi-arid climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_semi-arid_climate "Cold semi-arid climate") ([Köppen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen-Geiger_climate_classification_system "Köppen-Geiger climate classification system"): _BSk_), bordering on a [subtropical highland climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical_highland_climate "Subtropical highland climate") ([Köppen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen-Geiger_climate_classification_system "Köppen-Geiger climate classification system"): _Cwb_). The characteristic of the climate is an extended dry season that runs from May until October with a wet season that generally begins in November with the principal rains ending in March.

The valley of Cochabamba has been classified as a [mesothermal valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesothermal_valley "Mesothermal valley").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-geohi-17) The basin floor has an average elevation of 2600 m but at its lowest point in the east it runs at 2480 m.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-geohi-17) Surrounding mountains vary in height with the highest elevation in vicinity of valley being [Tunari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunari_(Bolivia) "Tunari (Bolivia)") with 5,023 m a.s.l.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-geohi-17) The city is primarily built on the [Cenozoic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenozoic "Cenozoic") and more specifically, [Quaternary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternary "Quaternary")[sedimentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sediment "Sediment") fill of the basin-valley.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-geohi-17) Mountains and hills are composed of old rocks dating to the [Paleozoic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleozoic "Paleozoic") and, in some parts, to the [Cretaceous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretaceous "Cretaceous").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-geohi-17)

According to the 2024 Bolivian census, the population of the municipality of Cochabamba is 665,505 inhabitants.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-27) This makes it the fourth most populous municipality in the country, behind [Santa Cruz de la Sierra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra "Santa Cruz de la Sierra"), [El Alto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Alto "El Alto"), and [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz "La Paz").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-28)

The population of the municipality increased by more than half between 1992 and 2024:

At the beginning of the republican era, Cochabamba ranked as the second most populated city in Bolivia according to the 1846 census, with a total of 30,396 inhabitants, behind La Paz, which had more than 60,000 inhabitants at that time.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-29)

The city extends beyond the political-administrative boundaries of the municipality of Cochabamba, forming a conurbation with the municipalities of [Colcapirhua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colcapirhua_Municipality "Colcapirhua Municipality"), [Quillacollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quillacollo_Municipality "Quillacollo Municipality"), [Sacaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacaba "Sacaba"), [Sipe Sipe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sipe_Sipe_Municipality "Sipe Sipe Municipality"), [Tiquipaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiquipaya_Municipality "Tiquipaya Municipality"), and [Vinto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinto_Municipality "Vinto Municipality"). Together they make up the Kanata Metropolitan Region, which is the third-largest metropolitan area in Bolivia and an important tourist, economic, industrial, and population center.

Like other Bolivian urban centers, Cochabamba is no exception to the national trend of urban growth at the expense of the rural population. This process of accelerated urbanization is not due exclusively to industrialization, but also to complex political and social factors such as poverty, the decline of the agricultural sector, and the availability of job opportunities in cities.

## Culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Culture")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Cultura_Cochabambina.jpg/250px-Cultura_Cochabambina.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cultura_Cochabambina.jpg)

Traditional clothing of Cochabamba

In Cochabamba, one of the most important religious festivities in Bolivia is held: that of the Virgin of Urkupiña, also known as the Patroness of National Integration. This celebration brings together Catholics from all over the country as well as foreign pilgrims, who participate either as spectators or as dancers in the folkloric procession of the same name, immersing themselves in the dual nature of a religious and traditional celebration. Another important festivity is the Alasitas Fair and the Corso de Corsos.

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Silpancho_cochalo.jpg/250px-Silpancho_cochalo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Silpancho_cochalo.jpg)

_[Sillp’ancho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silpancho "Silpancho") cochabambino_

The cuisine of Cochabamba is characterized by its great variety of culinary dishes. Since 2017, Cochabamba has been part of UNESCO's Creative Cities Network in the category of gastronomy.

*   **Chicharrón**: a dish made with pork cooked for approximately 5 to 6 hours, served with cooked corn hominy (_mote_) and potatoes.
*   **P’ampaku**: a dish prepared with chicken, pork, duck, potato, sweet potato, and plantain. All these ingredients are placed in a hermetically sealed container and buried in a pit, which is covered with stones and bricks previously heated by a wood or charcoal fire until the stones crack. It is covered with fresh grass or banana leaves and then completely sealed with mud. The food is considered cooked when the pit cracks and smoke rises from the burned fresh grass. It is served with a fresh vegetable salad.
*   **Pichón de Cliza**: a dish made with pigeon meat (squab), boiled and then grilled. It is served with rice and boiled potatoes.
*   **[Sillp’ancho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silpancho "Silpancho")**: a dry dish with breaded beef, pan-fried, accompanied by a fried egg and a raw salad of onion, carrot, tomato, and _locoto_. It is served with rice and boiled potatoes, which are later sliced and fried.
*   **Lapping**: a dish with fried marinaded flank steak.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-30)
*   **Jak’a Lawa**: a dish made from ground _choclo_ (fresh corn on the cob), accompanied by pieces of meat and pork rind. It is served in a deep plate.
*   **Ch’aqchu**: a dish made with _chuño_, meat boiled in water with potatoes and fava beans, hard-boiled eggs, fresh cheese sliced into rounds, and a salad of tomato and raw onion, all topped with a spicy red chili sauce.
*   **Jawas Piqtu**: a dish made with fava beans mixed with egg and tomato. It is served with potatoes.
*   **Pique Macho**: originally a dish made of beef loin fried in its own juices, with French fries, and a salad of tomato, onion, _locoto_, and sliced hard-boiled egg. The French fries are placed on the plate first, then the meat and chorizo are mixed and placed on top, and finally the salad and egg. A typical accompaniment is a mixture of oil, vinegar, salt, _llajua_, and finally beer, all mixed in a glass and then poured over the dish.
*   **Chank’a de conejo**: rabbit meat cut into pieces and boiled together with a white soup containing green onion (scallion), white potato, vegetables, and seasoned with traditional _llajwa_.
*   **Uchuku Aiquileño**: a dish consisting of red chili pepper, potatoes, rice, _chuño_, and meats (beef tongue, duck, and chicken). It is served with a chicken soup with chili (thickened with trimmings or ground bread), accompanied by rice cake, _ch’uñu phuti_, potato cake, fried ceibo flowers (_chilliqchi_), white potatoes, chicken meat, beef tongue, and golden-browned duck.
*   **[Llajua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llajua "Llajua")**: a spicy sauce made from _locoto_, tomato, and _quilquiña_ (an aromatic herb). The vast majority of traditional Bolivian dishes are accompanied by this sauce.

The international street art festival known as the BAU (Bienal de Arte Urbano) has been hosted in Cochabamba every two years since 2011. The festival is organized by proyecto mARTadero, a local cultural centre. In 2011, 2013, 2015, and 2017 the painting was done in the Villa Coronilla, and Geronimo de Osorio neighbourhoods. In 2019 the festival focused on the neighbourhood Esperanza, on the edge of the [Alalay Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alalay_Lake "Alalay Lake"). The festival has featured internationally renowned artists such as [Blu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blu_(artist) "Blu (artist)") (Italy) and Inti (Chile).[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-31)

Commensurate with other large cities in the Andean highlands of South America, Cochabamba is a city of contrasts. Its central commercial districts, Zona Norte, is bounded by Plaza Colón and Plaza 14 de Septiembre, are generally equipped with modern urban amenities and are where the majority of the city's formal business and commercial industries are based. La Cancha, the largest open-air market in South America, is also an active place where locals can buy a range of items.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-32) An active nightlife is centered around Calle España and along the broad, tree-lined boulevard, El Prado. In contrast, the Zona Sur, a remote area adjacent to the Wilstermann International Airport is visibly impoverished, with adobe homes and unpaved roads, which is often the first impression visitors acquire while commuting into the city.

In 2009, the government under President Evo Morales created a new constitution that declared Spanish and 36 other indigenous languages as the official languages of the country.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-:2-33) However, the most widely spoken languages in Cochabamba are Spanish and Quechua. Although the Spanish that is spoken in the Cochabamba region is generally regarded as rather conservative in its phonetics and vocabulary, the use of Quechua terminology (_wawa_ [child] and _wistupiku_ [mouth or twist lips][[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-34)) has been widely incorporated into its standardized form.

About four-fifths of the population of Bolivia identifies as Catholic.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-:2-33)

Like other cities that share the same ethnic group quadrants like [Salta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salta "Salta") or [Cuenca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuenca,_Ecuador "Cuenca, Ecuador"), Cochabamba's demographics consist of the following visible groups in order of prevalence: Indigenous (mostly of [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_people "Quechua people") and [Aymara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_people "Aymara people") ethnicity) people, [Mestizo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo"), or mixed Indigenous and Spanish European, and people of Spanish ([Criollos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criollo_(people) "Criollo (people)")) and other European descent. As well as a fairly significant population of [Afro-Bolivians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Bolivians "Afro-Bolivians").

By 2013, the human development index of the Metropolitan region of Cochabamba was 0.801 as a result of a 35% growth in the last 20 years.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-undp-3)

## Government

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Government")]

Departmental Government of Cochabamba 

### Capital status

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Capital status")]

Cochabamba is the capital of the department of Cochabamba and the seat of the Autonomous Departmental Government of Cochabamba, the political and administrative authority of the department. Following the enactment of the Popular Participation Law No. 1551 in 1994, together with the Administrative Decentralization Law No. 1654, a process of reconfiguration between the State and civil society was initiated, transferring powers and resources to subnational levels, such as municipal governments. As a result, Bolivia's departments enjoy autonomy statutes that define their internal structure. At the parliamentary level, the executive branch is headed by a governor, while the legislative branch is exercised by a [departmental legislative assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Bolivia "Politics of Bolivia"). In addition to the governor's office and several directorates, the Autonomous Departmental Government of Cochabamba is made up of eight departmental secretariats.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-35) The status of being the capital constitutes a distinguishing factor in relation to the other cities of the department, due to the higher concentration of public officials and a larger floating population that comes to Cochabamba to carry out procedures with the different secretariats and directorates.

Cochabamba is also the capital of the [Cercado Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cercado_Province_(Cochabamba) "Cercado Province (Cochabamba)"), located in the center of the department, since its founding on August 15, 1571 by the Spanish captain Gerónimo de Osorio under the original name Villa Real de Oropesa.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-37) This means that the various provincial delegations of the departments of the Autonomous Departmental Government and institutions of the Government of Bolivia are located in the city.

### Municipal government

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Municipal government")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Alcald%C3%ADa_Municipal_de_Cbba.jpg/250px-Alcald%C3%ADa_Municipal_de_Cbba.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alcald%C3%ADa_Municipal_de_Cbba.jpg)

Cochabamba City Hall

The administration of the city is carried out through democratic governance, whose authorities are elected every four years by universal suffrage. The electoral roll is made up of all registered residents of Cochabamba who are over 18 years of age and Bolivian nationals. The Mayor of Cochabamba is the head of government and of the municipal administration, legally representing the municipality in judicial and extrajudicial matters. The mayor also presides over the executive branch of the city.

According to Article 283 of the Political Constitution of the State and Law No. 482 on Autonomous Municipal Governments, municipal government consists of the Municipal Council, which exercises legislative, deliberative, and oversight powers, in cooperation with the executive branch.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-38) The Cochabamba Municipal Council is composed of eleven councilors elected by direct vote in municipal elections and represents the highest legislative authority of the municipal government. Decisions and resolutions are adopted by a majority vote or by a two-thirds majority, depending on the general regulations.

Since May 3, 2021, the Mayor of Cochabamba has been former presidential candidate and businessman [Manfred Reyes Villa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Reyes_Villa "Manfred Reyes Villa") ([APB Súmate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/APB_S%C3%BAmate "APB Súmate")).[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-39)

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Economy")]

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Muyurina%2C_Cochabamba.jpg/250px-Muyurina%2C_Cochabamba.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Muyurina,_Cochabamba.jpg)

Muyurina Skyline 

Cochabamba ranks third in economic importance nationwide. Historically, Cochabamba's economy was supported by agriculture. Currently, it has diversified and relies more on oil production and manufacturing. The municipality's economy is primarily centered on the [tertiary sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Services_sector "Services sector"), with activities such as commerce, transportation, storage, and other services, followed by the manufacturing industry. In 2021, the municipal Gross Domestic Product (GDP) was estimated to reach approximately 17,535 million [bolivianos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boliviano_(currency)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Boliviano (currency) (page does not exist)") (equivalent to US$6,710 million in [purchasing power parity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purchasing_power_parity "Purchasing power parity") terms), with a [GDP per capita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GDP_per_capita "GDP per capita") of 20,844 bolivianos (US$7,977 PPP).[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-:2-33) According to these figures, the municipality's economy contributes 43.6% of the department's value added and 6% of the national economy. During the heyday of the mining industry in [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"), Cochabamba enjoyed sustained development, only to enter a period of decline during the 18th century, as the silver mining industry began to decline. However, during the second half of the 19th century it was established as an agricultural center in the country.

The city's central area is where most of its businesses and commercial activity is concentrated. A large amount of formal and informal commerce is present on the streets of Cochabamba, encompassing the popular commercial area known as [La Cancha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Cancha "La Cancha"), made up of several private and public markets. However, its growth has begun to displace the commercial center to the northwest of the city, traditionally considered a residential area. It has a vibrant cosmopolitan nightlife, especially around Calle España and along the boulevard or avenue El Prado.

The city is home to many of the country's largest and most important companies, such as Boliviana de Aviación, ELFEC, Comteco, MotorParts, IC Norte, and large establishments such as Hipermaxi, Paseo Aranjuez, Hupermall, Supermall, and Mall Brisas del Sur, among others.

Cochabamba is the third-largest economy in Bolivia and is the most stable due to the dynamism of its market and domestic consumption, as well as its excellent transportation system, which allows it to transport goods to all of the department's provinces.

At the end of April and beginning of May of each year, the [Alalay Fairgrounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alalay_Fairgrounds?action=edit&redlink=1 "Alalay Fairgrounds (page does not exist)") opens its doors for eleven days exclusively to hold trade fair events of all kinds, with FEICOBOL (Cochabamba International Fair) being one of the largest commercial events in [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia") and its activities brought together companies worldwide, which helped the economy of the department and the growth of tourism. It was currently replaced by the Cochabamba International Exhibition Fair or FEXCO in an agreement between the [Autonomous Municipal Government of Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_Municipal_Government_of_Cochabamba?action=edit&redlink=1 "Autonomous Municipal Government of Cochabamba (page does not exist)") and the Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Services of Cochabamba (ICAM), which began its activities with its first version, held in 2023.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-40)

### Agriculture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Agriculture")]

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Cochabamba_1988.jpg/250px-Cochabamba_1988.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cochabamba_1988.jpg)

The Cochabamba Valley around 1987

Agriculture in the city of Cochabamba was very important, but it has declined due to the expansion of the urban area, which has reduced the arable land south of the city, to the Maica and Tamborada areas. However, in the city's markets, you can buy products that vary depending on the area from which they are brought, from regions with a distant climate and geography:

*   **The Tropics**: in this area, the crops of [banana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musa_%C3%97_paradisiaca "Musa × paradisiaca"), orange, [mandarin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandarin_orange "Mandarin orange"), palm heart, papaya, pineapple, cocoa, etc. are mainly found.
*   **The valleys**, this is the main agricultural area, in this area there are crops of [broad bean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicia_faba "Vicia faba"), [pea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pisum_sativum "Pisum sativum"), onion, corn, tomato, [locoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locoto "Locoto"), [parsley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsley "Parsley"), lettuce, [turnip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turnip "Turnip"), carrot, [custard apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Custard_apple "Custard apple"), [strawberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fragaria "Fragaria"), [peach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prunus_persica "Prunus persica"), etc.

*   **Subyungas**, in this area there are mainly crops of [broad bean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicia_faba "Vicia faba"), peas, custard apple and potato.

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Transport")]

The metropolitan area of Cochabamba (Vinto, Tiquipaya, Quillacollo, Colcapirhua, Cochabamba and Sacaba) has an extensive transportation system, which cover all the districts.

There are almost 70 bus and minibus lines, from A to Z, and dozens of minibuses and fixed-route trufis (T.RU.FI, or "taxi con ruta fija") taxi lines. Most lines have [GPS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPS "GPS") system for monitoring and regulation of hour (line 1, line 16, line L, Line 3V, line 20, line 30, etc.). The T.RU.FI service has at least 60 lines; they are identified by signs on the roof of the vehicle showing the route from the initial stop until the final stop, which is also indicated by the line number to which it belongs.

## Municipal waste

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Municipal waste")]

EMSA, the municipal sanitation company, is responsible for the pickup, transportation, storage and removed from urban waste produced. EMSA covers 88% of the city and collects 400 tonnes of waste produced per day.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-Botaderos18Apr-42) Through the municipal government of Cochabamba, special containers made available throughout the city for the storage of solid waste common. The municipality's sole disposal facility, the K'ara K'ara waste dump (Botadero K'ara K'ara), has been the centre of a long-running controversy over pollution of the air and groundwater; it is frequently blockaded by neighbouring residents demanding changes.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-Botaderos18Apr-42)

## Additional notes of interest

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cochabamba&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Additional notes of interest")]

*   Cochabamba is also mentioned in the documentary _[The Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Corporation\_(2003\_film) "The Corporation (2003 film)")_, about their fight against the privatisation of water by a foreign-owned company, against which the people protested and won. The privatisation had gone to such an extent that even rainwater was not allowed to be collected. Read [Cochabamba protests of 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_protests_of_2000 "Cochabamba protests of 2000").
*   Cochabamba was featured as a location in the story in the 1983 film, _[Scarface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarface\_(1983\_film) "Scarface (1983 film)")_. Powerful drug lord [Alejandro Sosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alejandro_Sosa "Alejandro Sosa") resided there, governed large coca plantations and owned cocaine labs whereupon further refining, would be shipped to [Tony Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Montana "Tony Montana") in Florida.
*   Cochabamba is the setting of the 2010 movie _[También la Lluvia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tambi%C3%A9n\_la\_Lluvia "También la Lluvia")_ (_Even the rain_), which takes place during the water war of 2000. It depicts a crew making a movie about the colonization of Latin America when the protests against privatization erupt. The film stars Mexican actor [Gael García Bernal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gael_Garc%C3%ADa_Bernal "Gael García Bernal"), and received positive reviews.
*   Cochabamba is also the site of several major spammers, as confirmed by the watchdog group Spamhaus.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba#cite_note-43)

[Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguay "Paraguay") consists of 17 [departments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_(administrative_division) "Department (administrative division)") ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _departamentos_; singular – _departamento)_ and [one capital district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asunci%C3%B3n "Asunción") (_distrito capital_). The country is divided into two non-official regions: The "Occidental Region" or Chaco (Boquerón, Alto Paraguay and Presidente Hayes), and the "Oriental Region" or Parana (other departments and the capital district).

[Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguay "Paraguay") consists of 17 [departments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_(administrative_division) "Department (administrative division)") ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _departamentos_; singular – _departamento)_ and [one capital district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asunci%C3%B3n "Asunción") (_distrito capital_). The country is divided into two non-official regions: The "Occidental Region" or Chaco (Boquerón, Alto Paraguay and Presidente Hayes), and the "Oriental Region" or Parana (other departments and the capital district).

**Alto Paraguay** (Spanish pronunciation:[[ˈalto paɾaˈɣwaj]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish"); _Upper Paraguay_) is the least populous [department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_(subnational_entity) "Department (subnational entity)") of [Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguay "Paraguay"). The capital is the town of [Fuerte Olimpo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuerte_Olimpo "Fuerte Olimpo").

In 1992, the Chaco Department was merged with Alto Paraguay.

## Nature and national parks

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alto_Paraguay_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Nature and national parks")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Black_jaguar.jpg/250px-Black_jaguar.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Black_jaguar.jpg)

The Jaguar inhabits all of Alto Paraguay's national parks

Alto Paraguay contains many natural resources, so is home to several [national parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks "National parks"), each with different characteristics. The [Defensores del Chaco National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parque_Nacional_Defensores_del_Chaco?action=edit&redlink=1 "Parque Nacional Defensores del Chaco (page does not exist)") is the largest in the Paraguayan territory and holds the hill [Cerro León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Le%C3%B3n?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cerro León (page does not exist)"), the highest point in northern Paraguay. The dry terrain optimally grows various species of [cactus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cactus "Cactus"). [Parque Nacional Río Negro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parque_Nacional_R%C3%ADo_Negro?action=edit&redlink=1 "Parque Nacional Río Negro (page does not exist)") is an area with several small lakes and most of the department's [fauna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauna "Fauna"). In the dry regions are [Parque Nacional Coronel Cabrera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parque_Nacional_Coronel_Cabrera?action=edit&redlink=1 "Parque Nacional Coronel Cabrera (page does not exist)") and [Parque Nacional Chovoreca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parque_Nacional_Chovoreca?action=edit&redlink=1 "Parque Nacional Chovoreca (page does not exist)").

## Agriculture, livestock and deforestation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alto_Paraguay_Department&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Agriculture, livestock and deforestation")]

[![Image 10: Map of Alto Paraguay showing tree-cover loss years, with forest remaining since 2000 in green and loss years shaded yellow through purple.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Alto_Paraguay%2C_2001-2024.png/330px-Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Alto_Paraguay%2C_2001-2024.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Alto_Paraguay,_2001-2024.png)

Tree-cover loss year in Alto Paraguay, 2001-2024, from the [Global Forest Change dataset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Forest_Change_dataset "Global Forest Change dataset").

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/Sorghum_linea_14_Alto_Paraguay.jpg/250px-Sorghum_linea_14_Alto_Paraguay.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sorghum_linea_14_Alto_Paraguay.jpg)

Sorghum harvest 2008, Linea 14, Agua Dulce Region

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Sugarcane_cultivation_Alto_Paraguay.JPG/250px-Sugarcane_cultivation_Alto_Paraguay.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sugarcane_cultivation_Alto_Paraguay.JPG)

Sugar cane, Linea 14, Agua Dulce Region

Paraguay's largest reserves of undeveloped fertile forest and lowest land prices are found in Alto Paraguay. Agriculture and cattle farming have started to make inroads. The fertility of the Chaco's deep sedimentary soils is generally high, except in the westernmost parts, where there are very sandy soils, and in the eastern plain where there are some seasonal wetlands. Annual rainfall is sufficient in the east (around 1200 mm), fair in the center (around 900 mm) and scarce in the west (around 700 mm). A lack of infrastructure and roads is the primary limitation for farmers in the area.

Current agricultural expansion comes at the expense of the area's native forests. During the two decades between 1990 and 2010, Paraguay had one of the highest [deforestation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deforestation "Deforestation") rates worldwide. The [World Land Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Land_Trust "World Land Trust") estimated 2008 deforestation in the Paraguay Chaco was over 200,000 hectares. [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alto_Paraguay_Department#cite_note-2)

The department's most important activity is cattle ranching, extensive in the savannas of the east and intensive on the planted pastures of cleared land. Cultivation of sorghum, sugar cane and (in planning stage as of January 2009, for the arid west) [jatropha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jatropha "Jatropha") are very recent developments.

**Alto Paraguay** (Spanish pronunciation:[[ˈalto paɾaˈɣwaj]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish"); _Upper Paraguay_) is the least populous [department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_(subnational_entity) "Department (subnational entity)") of [Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguay "Paraguay"). The capital is the town of [Fuerte Olimpo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuerte_Olimpo "Fuerte Olimpo").

In 1992, the Chaco Department was merged with Alto Paraguay.

## Nature and national parks

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alto_Paraguay_Department&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Nature and national parks")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Black_jaguar.jpg/250px-Black_jaguar.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Black_jaguar.jpg)

The Jaguar inhabits all of Alto Paraguay's national parks

Alto Paraguay contains many natural resources, so is home to several [national parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks "National parks"), each with different characteristics. The [Defensores del Chaco National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parque_Nacional_Defensores_del_Chaco?action=edit&redlink=1 "Parque Nacional Defensores del Chaco (page does not exist)") is the largest in the Paraguayan territory and holds the hill [Cerro León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Le%C3%B3n?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cerro León (page does not exist)"), the highest point in northern Paraguay. The dry terrain optimally grows various species of [cactus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cactus "Cactus"). [Parque Nacional Río Negro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parque_Nacional_R%C3%ADo_Negro?action=edit&redlink=1 "Parque Nacional Río Negro (page does not exist)") is an area with several small lakes and most of the department's [fauna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauna "Fauna"). In the dry regions are [Parque Nacional Coronel Cabrera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parque_Nacional_Coronel_Cabrera?action=edit&redlink=1 "Parque Nacional Coronel Cabrera (page does not exist)") and [Parque Nacional Chovoreca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parque_Nacional_Chovoreca?action=edit&redlink=1 "Parque Nacional Chovoreca (page does not exist)").

## Agriculture, livestock and deforestation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alto_Paraguay_Department&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Agriculture, livestock and deforestation")]

[![Image 10: Map of Alto Paraguay showing tree-cover loss years, with forest remaining since 2000 in green and loss years shaded yellow through purple.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Alto_Paraguay%2C_2001-2024.png/330px-Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Alto_Paraguay%2C_2001-2024.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Global_Forest_Change_tree-cover_loss_year_in_Alto_Paraguay,_2001-2024.png)

Paraguay's largest reserves of undeveloped fertile forest and lowest land prices are found in Alto Paraguay. Agriculture and cattle farming have started to make inroads. The fertility of the Chaco's deep sedimentary soils is generally high, except in the westernmost parts, where there are very sandy soils, and in the eastern plain where there are some seasonal wetlands. Annual rainfall is sufficient in the east (around 1200 mm), fair in the center (around 900 mm) and scarce in the west (around 700 mm). A lack of infrastructure and roads is the primary limitation for farmers in the area.

Current agricultural expansion comes at the expense of the area's native forests. During the two decades between 1990 and 2010, Paraguay had one of the highest [deforestation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deforestation "Deforestation") rates worldwide. The [World Land Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Land_Trust "World Land Trust") estimated 2008 deforestation in the Paraguay Chaco was over 200,000 hectares. [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alto_Paraguay_Department#cite_note-2)

The department's most important activity is cattle ranching, extensive in the savannas of the east and intensive on the planted pastures of cleared land. Cultivation of sorghum, sugar cane and (in planning stage as of January 2009, for the arid west) [jatropha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jatropha "Jatropha") are very recent developments.

## **Backpacking in Cochabamba**

👍 Recommended city ranked #5

By Johan Kruseman 🇳🇱 | Updated September 23, 2026

You land in Cochabamba and hit your first real fork: do you burn time and comfort on a 7–8 hour night bus from La Paz to save cash, or pay more for a quick flight and arrive with energy to actually enjoy the city? That single decision sets the tone for your whole stay, because Cochabamba rewards the traveler who arrives ready to move, eat, and explore.   
  
Cochabamba sits in central Bolivia, in a broad valley between the high Andes and the lowlands. For backpackers, it’s a slow-burn city: cheap food portions that could feed a small army, a relaxed main square, the Cristo de la Concordia viewpoint, and a lived-in, local feel rather than a curated “experience.” It’s easier and safer than El Alto or parts of La Paz, but less instantly social than Sucre. You work a bit harder to meet people, but your money goes far and the city feels real, not staged.

1.   **Cristo de la Concordia** — The giant hilltop statue that watches over the city; climb the long stairway (or take the cable car when it’s running) for one of the best panoramas of Cochabamba and a real sense of local pride.
2.   **Plaza 14 de Septiembre & Catedral Metropolitana** — The civic heart: people-watching, street vendors, and the cathedral’s colonial façade. Shows you how Cochabamba life centers around public space.
3.   **Mercado La Cancha** — Massive, messy, and addictive market where you can eat cheap local food, buy crafts, and see everyday Bolivian commerce up-close. Great for photos and for probing Bolivian food culture.
4.   **Palacio Portales** — Patiño’s early 20th-century mansion: ornate rooms, ironwork, and gardens that reveal the region’s mining wealth and quirky history. It’s a quieter, oddly elegant contrast to the city center.
5.   **Laguna Alalay** — An urban lagoon with a walking/cycling path and surprising birdlife. Perfect for a relaxed afternoon away from traffic and for seeing locals exercise and hang out.
6.   **Museo de Historia Natural “Alcides d’Orbigny”** — Small but solid natural history collection (local geology, fauna, fossils). Good if you want context on the region’s landscapes and biodiversity without leaving the city.
7.   **Museo Arqueológico (Universidad Mayor de San Simón)** — University-run archaeology displays with ceramics, tools, and regional pre-Columbian material — useful background before exploring nearby ruins or terraces.
8.   **El Prado (Paseo del Prado)** — The tree-lined main promenade with cafes, statues and a relaxed vibe. Best for a late-afternoon stroll and for watching Cochabambinos take their time.
9.   **La Recoleta** — A hilltop neighborhood with a small convent/mirador and excellent city views; less touristy than Cristo and great at sunset for photos and a quieter vantage point.
10.   **Museo Antonio Paredes Candia** — Housed in an old mansion, this museum celebrates Bolivian folklore, popular literature and daily life—useful to understand local culture beyond the headlines.

A few solid day trips near Cochabamba: Tunari National Park for hiking and highland scenery (personal favorite), the archaeological ruins at Sipe Sipe, and the pilgrimage town of Quillacollo (Urkupiña festival and local markets).

In the afternoon, make your way to the charming neighborhood of Cala Cala. Here, you can visit the Museo de Historia Natural, which showcases Bolivia’s diverse ecosystems. It’s often overlooked by tourists, but the exhibits are fascinating and give you a deeper understanding of the country’s natural beauty.  
  
As evening approaches, return to the city center and explore the Plaza 14 de Septiembre. Grab dinner at a local eatery, where you can try pique a lo macho, a hearty dish of beef, sausage, and potatoes. The plaza comes alive at night, with street performers and locals enjoying the cool air.   
  
Cochabamba may not be the first stop on everyone’s itinerary, but it’s a city that rewards those who take the time to explore. Each moment spent here adds a layer to your travel experience, making it all the more memorable.
